Mr. GEORGE BLACK (Yukon) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 44, to amend the Yukon Act.
He said: The object of the proposed amendment is to increase the classes of actions in which litigants may have the right to appeal and may have the right to have issues of fact determined by a juiy. Before the Yukon courts litigants are limited to appealing from final judgments only; there is no right to appeal from interlocutory judgments. Members of the House who are lawyers will realize that is a most unnecessary limitation. The right to appeal in Yukon courts is limited to actions where the amount in controversy is $500 or upwards; where the title to real estate is in question, where the validity of a patent is affected, or the matter in question relates to the taking of an annual rent, a customary or other duty or fee, or a like demand of a public or general nature affecting future rights, or in cases of proceedings for or upon mandamus, prohibition or injunction. Strange to say, cases which most frequently arise there do not come within the list of those in which the right of appeal exists, namely: Actions for the recovery of mining claims, both placer gold claims and quartz claims; actions to establish the title to mining claims and actions to settle boundaries of mining claims. The court has jurisdiction to try actions for divorces and judicial separation, but there is no right of appeal. The same limitations apply to the right to have questions of fact

Hon. C. A. STEWART (Acting Minister of Immigration and Colonization) moved to introduce Bill No. 45, respecting Chinese Immigration.
He said: There are several new features in this bill. One is that we are by statute limiting entrance of Chinese to Canada to mem; bers of the diplomatip corps; to children born in Canada but who have left this country for the purpose of being educated; and to merchants . and students.
It is rather a difficult matter to define the word "merchants" and we have not made a very definite description of the individual to be known to a merchant who will be admitted to Canada. Undoubtedly there will be a considerable amount of discussion on this particular section when the bill comes up for consideration. The definition of "students" is restricted to students coming to Canada for the purpose of attending any Canadian university or college authorized by statute or charter to confer degrees. While we have had some difficulty in connection with the definition of "merchants," we have defined students very clearly.
These are the two important clauses of the bill. There are many other regulations to be dealt with, but they will come up for consideration in Committee of the Whole and will be dealt with there.

I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Justice to some things that have happened during the past year in connection with capital punishment. We have had capital punishment in this country for a long time, and it is possible we shall not abolish it at the present time. We had a case during the last year, in the county in which I live, of a man being executed in such a bungling manner that it was commented on, I think, by all the papers in Canada. I know there is a very strong feeling in my province, and I think in other provinces of Canada, that capital punishment should not be carried out at the county gaols, but that some provision should be made for executing prisoners who are condemned to death in the penitentiaries or at some central place in the province where proper arrangements can be made to carry out the law in that respect. Living in the county in which this bungling occurred last year, I feel that I would be remiss in my duty if I let this opportunity pass without calling the attention of the Minister of Justice to the matter. I have no doubt that he has received communications on the subject, and I should like to know whether it is the intention of his department to make arrangements to have executions caried out in future at the penitentiaries in Canada.

I would like to add a word along the same line as the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton. This matter has been brought very forcibly to the attention of the country by reason of the terrible bungling that took place in an execution in the county of Carleton, New Brunswick. A capital crime of some enormity was committed down there, and the death penalty was imposed upon the accused.	I quite
appreciate the fact that under the constitution the carrying out of the punishment for that offence is imposed upon the provincial authorities, and that in consequence a constitutional question arises in connection with my hon. friend's suggestion. The sheriffs are appointed by the provincial government, and for the most*part they are very fair officials and carry out their duties with a certain degree of exactness; but in the case of capi-

Supply-Justice
tal punishment almost invariably we find that they refuse to perform their duty. I am not casting any reflections upon the sheriff of Carleton county. He probably did what any other sheriff in the country would have done. He endeavoured to get some other person to perform the task that the law had imposed upon him, and so far as he failed to do it himself, he failed to perform his duty. At the same time, he employed a person who was evidently wholly unqualified with the result .that the whole community, the whole country, in fact, was shocked at the manner in which the punishment was inflicted in that case. It is not perhaps any business of the Dominion, strictly from a constitutional point of view, but it does occur to me that a convention or arrangement might be made with the provincial authorities whereby the imposition of capital punishment might very well be carried out by officials of the Dominion in the penitentiaries at the various centres. I hope that the Minister of Justice to whom I have already spoken about this matter will give it his very best consideration. The country will not stand for a repetition of what took place in Carleton, New Brunswick, last year.

I want tb emphasize the remarks made by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) in connection with a hanging that took place in New Brunswick last summer. What took place on that occasion was very unfortunate; somebody is to blame, and I hope the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin), in the near future, will have the law of our province altered so that a man convicted and sentenced to be hanged will be hanged in the yard of the penitentiary, and not in the yard of the county gaol. Moreover, the sheriff of a county is not a competent man to hang one of his fellowmen. The man who should look after these serious matters ought to be appointed by the government of this country, and he ought to be the only man required to assume this duty.

In view of the discussion that has taken place regarding where the blame is to be attached for bungling the execution of a man in Carleton county, I should, perhaps, say another word. Our sheriff spared no effort to get a competent hangman and he secured a man recommended to him by the sheriff of Montreal as being competent. On the day before the execution was to take place, the sheriff received a telegram stating that on account of an accident, this man would be unable to attend. Our sheriff would not hang the man, and I
would be very sorry if he had to undertake such a duty. I do not think the sheriff of a county should be compelled to do the hanging for that county. He is an official who must perform his official duties and meet the people of his county in his every day official work.
This is part of his official duties.

Yes; but we should change it so that it should not be part of his official duties. Later on, he had the sentence postponed, because otherwise, under the Criminal Code, should the execution not have taken place on the day appointed, the man would have got off and could not be hanged afterwards. The sheriff came to Montreal and, for fear of a slip-up the next time, employed two men, each recommended to him as being competent to perform the hanging. He took them both down,- and I believe the hanging was carried out in a very efficient manner. The trouble was that the man was cut down before he was entirely dead. An investigation was held and the sheriff was exonerated from all blame in the matter. I think the investigation did not go deep enough; it did not place the blame where possibly it rightly belonged. Several surgeons were present who were testing the man to find out whether he was dead or not; but whether the surgeons pronounced him dead and he was * accordingly cut down, was not made clear. As the sheriff would not perform the hanging and had to employ another man, he must pay that man out of his own pocket. This is not fair. I do not think a sheriff is a competent man to hang a person; he is a man selected to do the duty of sheriff of a county in enforcing the law,' and unfortunately this is, at the present time, part of his duties. If executions were carried out at provincial penitentiaries, it would be well to have an efficient man to officiate for a province, or, possibly, for two provinces. I would not say as to that. You cannot expect every sheriff in every county to be an efficient hangman. Capital punishment is part of the law that I have never approved myself; but as it is on the statute books, if it is to be carried out, it should be carried out in an exemplary manner without a hitch, and this is not always the case at the present time. I hope the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) will see to it that this is arranged.

No one regrets more than I do this painful incident which was referred to; but as has been admitted by all



Supply-Justice
hon. members who have spoken, the carrying out of capital punishment is a matter in the jurisdiction of the provinces. We are told that it should not be the duty of a sherriff to carry out capital punishment. That may be so; but that is for the province to decide, and it is for the province to see that the sentence is carried out. A proposition is made that the executions should take place in provincial penitentiaries. First of all, there are no provincial penitentiaries. All our penitentiaries are Dominion. It has been suggested that, if possible, one penitentiary, where executions should take place, should be chosen for each part of the country. This is another matter that must be decided first by the provinces, and if the provinces ask us to lend a penitentiary for such executions, this is a matter which we might discuss and agree upon. I am disposed to do anything possible to prevent a repetition of such an incident. I understand that an investigation has taken place to find out where the responsibility for it rests. I have no comment to make as to the decision which was reached; but it is my intention to communicate with the different provinces and to try to find some way to give satisfaction to the people of Canada on this point.

I have always thought that it would be a wise provision, especially in the case of married convicts with dependents, that a portion of their earnings should be set aside for the maintenance of their families. I would like, by way of a little bit of healthy contrast, to call the attention of the minister to the hundreds of thousands of poor, honest and decent people in Canada who have to buy their own magazines and their own tobacco, and have to ggt along with very little help from the people who are so immensely anxious for the welfare of those who have struck sometimes at the very roots of society and are undergoing a just punishment. Then there is another grievance-shall Isay? -that the old veterans of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police have, and that is in connection with the veterans who served in the Riel Rebellion. All those of other branches, outside of the Mounted Police, who served in that rebellion received a land grant or scrip, but the officers and men I have referred to were not given any such recognition. This grievance has been brought to the attention of various governments and in calling attention to it now I do not do so in any spirit of criticism. I want the minister to recognize the fact that I am bringing it forward because I consider it to be a just claim. There are not, perhaps, very many of the survivors of that force left, most of them are pretty well advanced in years, but during all the intervening time they have made this claim and, in nearly every case, I think, have appealed to deaf ears. I think that we could well afford to do justice to these old veterans of this splendid police force. I am well aware that there are those in the country to-day who have some criticisms to offer of this force, but with that sentiment I have no sympathy whatever. But in order to meet their possible objection let me remind the committee that in relation to those in whose behalf I am pleading with the minister this afternoon there can be no such sentiment held. They were the pioneers in this great service, the men who, as practically every hon. gentleman from the prairie provinces knows, rode the plains and maintained law and order. In manj'- eases they were government, judiciary, police force, and general help for the settlers all through the West, and in my experience of some thirty years passing backwards and forwards over the prairies, and living also in the extreme West, I have witnessed'the extraordinary influence that these men gained over all classes of the community. Their deeds read like a romance; we all know that, and it is unecessary for me to bring forward any proof of it. I think, however, that the government of Canada should do justice to the remnants of this force, to those veterans who in their old age still feel that they were very unjustly treated.
Let me just bring forward one further argument ; I do not wish to labour the point. One of the reasons, it is alleged-and I have looked over the record pretty carefully,
and while I would not choose to pass a very decided opinion, I am inclined to sympathize wholly with them-one of the reasons alleged why they did not receive this scrip was because there was a little jealousy between the military commanders and the police force. There were strained relations to some extent, and the result was that while the police did perhaps some of the most difficult work in connection with that rebellion they received no recognition in the way of scrip, whereas all other branches of the service did. Years afterwards, it is true, a meagre attempt was made to do justice to them by striking a medal, which they all value very highly, but which certainly did not give them justice. I wish to ask the minister if he will again take their claims into consideration. I believe it is a just claim and one that ought to be granted. I just leave the matter in that way, and ask for his consideration.
Before sitting down I wish to refer to a kindred subject, and that is the meagre pension which is being paid to the widows of those who were in the service for many years. I have in my hand at the moment the case of the widow of a former superintendent, Mrs. Joseph Howe. Her husband was in the force for twenty-three years. He died in 1902. He went through the Riel rebellion and the South African war, and gave magnificent service all through his career in the force. His widow to-day is receiving a pension of $29.16 a month, and that is the widow of a man who attained the rank of superintendent while in the service. It is true that a very slight increase was made to this, perhaps, because of some action that was taken about a/year ago. But I am not basing my claim on this one case, I simply mention this as a typical case. There are widows, not a large number, it is true, who are receiving this meagre pension, which is based upon the very low rate of pay received by the force in those early days. I think the government could very well consider the claims of these persons for an increase in their pensions. The only argument against this claim that is worthy of any consideration at all is that if parliament were to raise the pension in conection with the Northwest Mounted Police force, we would have to raise the pension of all civil servants who are retired. In reply, I would submit to the minister that most of the civil servants who have been retired were retired under a very much higher rate of pay than the Northwest Mounted Police force. What I said two years ago, and also three years ago, when I spoke on this subject was that we should bring up the pensions of the

. veterans of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, and of their dependents who are drawing pensions, to some minimum standard at least, a minimum that would be in advance of what they are getting to-day and in some degree commensurate with the conditions that obtain now as compared with the conditions that obtained at that time. I bring the matter forward at this time for the attention of the minister, and hope that he will give it not only consideration, but, also that action for which he is known. I heard one of his friends describe him the other day as a man of few words but prompt action, and I believe that that virtue might very well be applied in these instances at this time.

Before the minister replies, I should like to endorse everything that has been said by my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). This matter has been before the House on several occasions. I know I have spoken on it once or twice. I happen to know some of the old veterans in my own constituency, and I know that the conditions prevailing there are such that they certainly require a little looking into. I understand that the number of these veterans in the Dominion at the present time is very small. These men gave the best part of their lives in the interests of opening up western Canada, and I think anyone who reads the history of the Northwest Mounted Police will admit that their record is hard to beat in any country. Some way, I think, could be found of getting around the difficulty mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, that the pensions of these men might be increased so as to make the evening of their lives a little more comfortable than it appears to be for some of them at present. It is not necessary for me to go into any details as my hon. friend has dealt with the matter fully, but I heartily endorse everything he has said and I trust that the minister will give the matter his very careful consideration.

I would like to call attention to what I regard as a very grave injustice in the administration and distribution [Sir Lomer Gouin.)
of bounties. There are three provinces in which we have productive oil wells, Ontario, New Brunswick and Alberta. In Alberta we have five producing oil wells, and there are nine more being drilled at the very extreme southern end of the province, with great prospects of success. New Brunswick has seven yielding oil wells, and Ontario had 3,015 in 1921. Now, let me draw attention to the fact that in the distribution of bounties Ontario received $90,751 in 1921, whilst New Brunswick received $3,926. On the other hand our men, who are operating under especially difficult conditions and are endeavouring to develop the oil resources in the Alberta fields, are receiving absolutely nothing. They have brought this matter to the attention of the department on several occasions in recent years but have received no consideration and no allowance. It seems that under the law a standard is fixed of specific gravity, and if there is any variation from that standard the producer' gets no share in this bounty. This seems to me to be directly contrary to what our policy should be. The drilling of these oil wells and the production of oil is one of the most important enterprises devolving upon this country at the present time.. Last year, for example, we imported over 366,000,000 gallons of crude oil whereas Canada itself produced only between five and six million gallons of oil. The needs of Canada for oil are very great. The country which produces and has an abundance of its own oil in future years is certainly going to take the lead in our civilization. This is a matter which we must not neglect and therefore these bounties should be granted in equal and equitable manner to all the provinces in which efforts are being made to develop this great resource. For the present I shall be satisfied with bringing the matter to the attention of the minister, and urging him to look into it and see that the bounty for the production of oil reaches the Alberta producers to the extent which they merit. When the budget is presented I shall deal with the question at greater length.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No later than yesterday my hon. friend brought to my notice, some changes which he thought would encourage the development of oil wells in western Canada. These will be taken into consideration by the government and a statement in that regard made when the budget is presented.
Respecting the matter of the bounty paid in different provinces the, reason for that is this. The bounty is based upon the specific gravity

Sup-ply-Trade and Commerce
of the oil produced, and those districts where the oil is not of such a standard as to entitle them to receive the. bounty, are protected under the tariff. We will take my hon. friend's observations under consideration.

I would like to draw the minister's attention to the fact that the crude oils we are producing in Alberta, regardless of the slight difference there might be in specific gravity as compared with other native oils, are available for all our uses in this country. We have our own refinery at Okotoks, and we are getting there the very best grade of gasoline, kerosene and all the various petroleum products. Under the circumstances I do not think we ought to be discriminated against in the manner which now obtains.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The reason which I have assigned explains why no bounty is given. However, we will look into the matter.

I would urge upon the minister the advisability of changing the specific gravity tests under which the bounty is paid. In Alberta the oil wells are drilled under very great difficulties. They are a long distance from the plants where the machinery and well casing are made, and the expense of putting down some of those wells runs into many thousands of dollars. I am sorry I have not the figures here. The wells are also very deep, in many cases reaching over three thousand feet. I think these facts should be taken into consideration when comparing the Alberta wells with the Ontario wells. I am told that the Ontario wells are comparatively shallow and that the drilling apparatus needed for them is very much cheaper. In Alberta a lot of men have had to give up drilling operations because of the great expense involved. I think the minister should take into consideration these facts, and either change the specific gravity test so that the Alberta oil wells may get the benefit of the bounty, or else do away with the bounty. I was told by*an oil operator that some of these oil wells miss coming under the provisions of the bounty by only a very slight percentage in the specific gravity test, and it seems to me very unfair that the Alberta oil men should be deprived of this assistance bearing in mind the very great disadvantages they are labouring under. In my opinion this is a case where the law needs revising, and if the government wishes to encourage the oil industry in Alberta it should make the change which we are suggesting.

While I am in favour of the bonuses provided for under this item,
I think the government might spend some money in another direction, more particularly in endeavouring to curb the operations of bogus oil companies which are selling, or endeavouring to sell, stocks to the people of this country. I know that out in our province we have a great many companies which are reporting in the newspapers from time to time that they are just about to strike oil. However, they have never struck any, yet they keep on taking money out of the pockets of the people. Now I know that there are hon. members who think that the people should be relieved of their money in some way-either by horse-racing, or by stocks, or otherwise- but I think this kind of thing is doing a great deal of harm, and the government should take steps to see that the public are not defrauded in the bare-faced, cold-blooded manner that a great many of these oil companies are guilty -of.

In full?

speechtext: Yes, but one firm contends that it is illegal.
Can the minister answer my question as to the reason for delay in bring-J ing on that case before the Supreme Court?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That, of course, is in the hands of the Justice department and I really could , not give my hon. friend the reason. I re-j member the circumstances he refers to and it | was stated that we would try and rush the | case through, but after the wheat board legis-j lation was put through the necessity for hurrying that case along was not as great and that is perhaps the reason for the delay. On February 16 the Justice department reported that the case was practically ready for trial and it was hoped to have it disposed of some time in the month of March.

I should like to draw the attention of the minister to one phase of the grain trade in western Canada which is very : much to the front in all discussions which are ! taking place there regarding the administra-I tion of the act, and that is with reference to dockage. I think possibly in our province at all events we had more dockage than usual , this year because we had an unusually good crop of weeds. I want to bring to the minister's attention the treatment I personally re-

ceived in regard to dockage of wheat, because it is typical of many cases that have happened this year. I shipped two cars of wheat to Vancouver in September and the dockage on both these cars was four per cent. I thought the dockage was excessive, and I wrote to the company who handled this grain and asked them to secure from the inspectors a statement showing how the dockage was made up.
I was informed in reply that the first car was a little better than two per cent cracked wheat and approximately two per cent seeds, the cracked wheat weighing up a little heavier than the seeds. The inspector's sample of the second car showed more seeds than the sample of the first car. The proportion worked out a little less than three per cent seeds as against a little over one per cent of cracked wheat. According to the statement which was sent me of the proceeds upon this car, we were paid the large sum' of one dollar per ton for these screenings. This wheat was shipped to Vancouver and cleaned there, and I am told there is no better market for chicken feed in Canada than Vancouver. Cracked wheat ought to be good for chicken feed, yet this dockage was sold for only one dollar per ton.
I made a complaint about this, and we afterwards received a money order for $8.50 covering these screenings at the rate of $4 per ton. On the other car, which I mentioned first, where there was something over two per cent of cracked wheat we have not received any- . thing over the one dollar per ton. I certainly think this is a matter demanding very thorough investigation by the department. I am not very well informed as to how this dockage is handled, but I have been told that in some of the government elevators there are two bins into which the dockage is put. In the one bin the dockage belongs to the government, that is, dockage under a certain percentage, which goes to the government elevator to pay for the cleaning. Where the dockage is over that percentage, it goes to the shipper of the grain and he is paid for that dockage according to the price at which it is sold. This goes into a separate bin. If that is the case, it rests with the management of the elevator where these screenings shall be put. I know that the charge is sometimes made that the management of the elevator will take screenings which may belong to some car where the dockage is over the percentage which would entitle them to take the screenings for cleaning charges, and this dockage may consist largely of cracked wheat and wild oats, and put that dockage into their own bin, and switch dockage from some other car which has weed seeds of no value, into the other bin. Possibly the minister would give

Supply-Trade and Commerce
us some information, regarding that. I should also like his promise that he will have a thorough investigation made as to the working of the elevator in Vancouver to see why so many shippers are being paid only one dollar per ton for good screenings.
As regards this question of dockage, I have had resolutions from three different farmers' associations in my constituency asking that it be made compulsory for country elevators to install proper cleaning facilities, so that all the wheat might be cleaned at the country elevator, and the dockage kept there and returned to the farmer. I know there are some objections to that; but I should like the minister to promise us that he will have the Board of Grain Commissioners make a very thorough investigation into this question of dockage and report to the House, at least by next year, whether that would be a good procedure. I saw in the Calgary Herald some time ago that it was estimated that the farmers of western Canada would pay freight, on screenings on 1922 crop, amounting to $5,000,000. Some means should be devised of saving freight on dockage, and I am quite convinced that if grain were cleaned at country elevators, the dockage that would be returned to the farmer would much more than pay for cleaning the grain. In some cases the dockage amounts to seven and, in odd cases, to ten per cent, so that, if the dockage were removed, hon. members can easily realize the saving to the railway companies in the fall in the number of cars required for hauling this grain.
I wish to emphasize again the question of dockage on grain that went to Vancouver this fall. I have had many complaints in my district in regard to it. We had a very dry summer; the wheat was unusually dry and brittle, and I believe it cracked worse than usual. Of course much of the cracked wheat is caused by inefficient threshers. When you have a separator cracking wheat, it is almost impossible to take the weed seeds out, as the cracked wheat will cover up the weed screens. There should be returned to the farmers of Alberta many thousands of dollars, jqst from dockage that was taken out of their grain this fall and for which they were paid, in many cases, as I was in my experience, as low as one dollar per ton. It is nothing less than downright robbery that screenings of the class I have' spoken of should be paid for at the rate of one dollar per ton.

I think the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) is very fortunate in getting one dollar per ton for his screenings.
I received only twenty-five cents per ton for mine. I cleaned my wheat in the elevator and shipped it to Fort William after it. was cleaned. On 2,142 bushels of wheat I had a dockage of 86 bushels and 40 pounds, for which I got 56 cents. I asked for a reinspection; but in the location where I live, namely, on the Canadian National going south from Winnipeg to Emerson, a branch goes direct to Port Arthur. My wheat leaves my home town and goes to Emerson and then direct to Port Arthur, and it is almost impossible to get a re-inspection unless wheat passes through Winnipeg. Can the minister state whether or not one can get a re-inspection when wheat does not pass through Winnipeg?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
It might be difficult to have an inspection after grain had passed an inspection point; but if the bulk had not been broken and the inspector advised in time, and the car held, I can see no reason why there should not be a re-inspection. The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) and the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beaubien) havte brought up a question of great importance to all Canada. No question causes more trouble in the administration of the Grain Act than this question of screenings. Not only is this question of interest to the people of western Canada, but I call the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) as a witness that it is of interest to the people of eastern Canada, because the good farmers of eastern Canada object very strenuously to having these dirty seeds, mixed or sold straight, and dirtying farms that are fairly well kept. I have considerable sympathy with the idea of having grain cleaned at the original point of shipment; but I am not sure that could be carried out in a new country, nor am I sure that the government would be wise, in the administration of the act, to make it obligatary upon all country elevators. It costs money to put in cleaning machinery, perhaps not so much to put it in as to operate it, and to clean fast enough so that the grain can be taken care of as it comes into the warehouse back in the country. I am told some modern threshing machines are now equipped with cleaning machinery that cleans the grain fairly well. I think I should say to my hon. friend that I have already been discussing this on two different occasions with the Board of Grain Commissioners, and we have tried to work out some plan whereby we might arrange to have grain cleaned economically, leaving the screenings back on the farm where they could be used near the point of produc-

Supply-Trade and Commerce
tion and thus saving the man who owns the grain the cost of freight shipping this to Fort William or to Vancouver where it is cleaned. There is not much sense in paying freight on screenings that are of comparatively small value.
The hon. member for Macleod brought up the question of the returns he had received, and I was astonished that he would only receive one dollar a ton for cracked wheat, because my experience has taught me that feed is worth considerably more than that. I agree with him that there should be some demand on the Pacific coast for, at least, a reasonable amount of chicken feed and a considerable quantity of mill feed. I have had brought to my attention a statement sent to us by the grain commissioners, a statement that was reliable and supported by a telegram from would-be customers. We did for a time find a very good market for these screenings in the United States. It was represented to the commission that the screenings were used largely for feeding sheep. We had men follow the screenings along, in the years past, to their point of destination, and we discovered that Canadian screenings were put into various grades of feed, some of them selling at very high prices under a fancy name. The United States, like Canada, in recent years have passed drastic legislation controlling the product that goes into different feeds, requiring an analysis, and the result of all this has been that they have destroyed the market for that sort of grain, grain which the hon. member for South Oxford called "rubbish." I have in my hand a memorandum from the Board of Grain Commissioners. I think I had better put on record the statement of the grain commissioners on this matter. They point out that the market for screenings is now limited, and I may say that it is not the operator of the elevator but the inspector who determines what dockage there shall be to bring wheat up to standard grade. The grain commissioners make this statement:
To-day the price paid is $1.50 per ton for general run screenings of which the proportion of anything better than refuse runs from 10 to 20 per cent the average percentage based on actual cleaning test being practically 15 per cent. As an example, take today's purchase price of $1.50 per ton, plus $2 per ton, cost of cleaning, equals $3.50; 15 per cent, better than refuse equals 300 lbs. per ton, at a price at which thousands of tons could be obtained, namely $9 per ton, equals $1.35, which shows a cost to the elevator, or an absolute loss of $2.15 per ton, as refuse screenings are offered f.o.b. cars free to any party who will take them away. As a matter of fact an entire boatload was offered recently to the Globe Elevator Company, Duluth, plus 50 cents per ton, providing they would 
take them from the elevator by boat. This company replied under date of October 13th as follows:
"Impossible work screenings to pay cost, evea basis
50 cents per ton credit, so will pass it up."
The actual facts-and I am citing now the conditions on lake Superior at Fort William and Port Arthur-show that the grain commissioners offered a bonus of 50 cents per ton if the screenings were taken away and their offer was refused. This refusal came from a market where heretofore we sold screenings by the boat load. I am therefore entirely in sympathy with the view of my hon. friend that something should be done to have grain cleaned at point of loading near the producer. I thank him for bringing the matter to our attention and I shall submit it again to the grain commissioners to see whether, during the year, we cannot work out some scheme. But it must be an economical scheme so that we shall not close up the elevators and in that way do more harm to the producer.

As the minister points out, the question of deciding where the grain should be cleaned is one that is difficult to settle. A good many people will remember that years ago the cleaning was done largely in the country elevators, but the very difficulty the minister has spoken of was experienced there. The grain is usually rushed in at certain hours of the day. There are hours of the day when very few loads arrive, and at other times there is a great rush; and if farmers thresh and haul their grain from the threshing machines to the elevator it is a considerable inconvenience to them to have to wait an hour or two before they can unload. I am not sure that it is practicable to have the cleaning done in the country elevator, although it would be a considerable economy if the freight could be saved and all the trouble referred to avoided. I have in mind two cases, in which I could give the names and addresses, of farmers who made the same complaint that has been raised by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote). In one case the farmer received 50 cents a ton for cleaned oats taken out of grain grown on new land, and in the other case $1 a ton was paid for cracked grain which was considered quite clean. I believe that what the minister said in regard to prices of screenings generally and the lack of market for them is true. But I think it is simply a case . of screenings and screenings. There are some screenings that are worth very little. By the time they pass through the terminal elevator, where there are facilities for putting them over the screen several times, they are practically nothing but wild oats and dirt and are worth little. A great

Supply-Trade and Commerce
deal of good grain, of course, has been taken out of such screenings. But the complaint is not in regard to that sort of screening, on which no one places very much value. The complaint is in reference to such cases as I have referred to and that mentioned by the hon. member for Macleod, where for cracked wheat and clean oat screenings that are worth $15 a ton 50 cents or $1 is offered. But this is only one of many complaints which I hope will be thoroughly investigated and remedied by the grain inquiry commission which we hope will be appointed later on.

Is it not possible to have machinery in the threshing outfits that would take the great proportion of the small seeds out of the grain and thus solve the difficulty at the very point where it can be done most easily and at least cost?

Probably the time will come when that will be done generally, but at present it is not practicable. There are very few threshing machines that are so equipped as properly to clean grain in the field, and I am inclined to think that for a number of years to come the difficulty will be this, that with the screenings a considerable quantity of good grain will be taken out in the field, which could be made use of in the terminal elevators. This grain could be extracted at the elevators but it cannot be separated in the field. These are difficulties for which I do not pretend to offer any solution offhand. I do not know what the solution will be, but it is a matter that calls for a great deal of care and thought because the farmers lose a good deal as things are.

I should be glad if the minister would promise to have the Board of Grain Commissioners make a thorough investigation into this matter of dockage at Vancouver. Many of us would like to get a few dollars out of the dockage which someone out there has kept from us. They have paid $1 a ton where the dockage was something worth while. In the particular car I referred to more than one-half was cracked wheat. The minister might see that the commissioners endeavour to get some justice for the men whiS had dockage that should have been adequately paid for and for which they were given only $1 a ton. When I received my statement I said I would rather they had not. offered me anything, because I considered it an insult to be offered a dollar per ton for screenings of that kind. I want to put on Hansard a statement which I got last year, through the Department of Trade and Commerce, from the Board of Grain Commissioners giving an analysis of the dockage on wheat received at the terminal elevators at Port William and Port Arthur for the crop year 1920-21. I shall read this statement in order to bring to the attention of the House and the people generally the amount of dockage that is being taken to Fort William and which should be left at home.

One other question. A year ago, if I remember correctly, I was told that we could not have our screenings reshipped from Calgary to local points, on account of regulations prohibiting their movement. Are such regulations in effect; and, if so, are they issued from the minister's department?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: In answer to the first question, the deputy minister already has a note of my hon. friend's complaint regarding the price ' paid at Vancouver and will to-morrow write the Grain Commission for an explanation. As to the second question, no such regulations have been issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce; but I think the Department of Agriculture issues regulations covering the shipment of noxious weeds.

During the course of the year I have had several complaints from farmers that they are not able to purchase screenings from the government elevator at Calgary. What disposition is made of these screenings? And why is it that local farmers are unable to purchase them?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I imagine if there is a market for the screenings in Calgary the elevator operators will be glad to sell them to local farmers. I shall draw the attention of the grain commissioners to this matter. Of course, where there is no local demand, screenings are sometimes used for fuel.

Apropos of what my colleague from Macleod (Mr. Coote) has been saying, I would call the attention of the minister to the value of these screenings in our mixed farming operations. I doubt if their value is sufficiently comprehended. We produced in what we call the Lethbridge freight district 22,000,000 bushels of wheat last year, constituting over one third of the entire wheat product of Alberta, and figuring the screenings at two per cent we would have about 450,000 bushels available if we had a storage elevator at say, Lethbridge, with proper cleaning facilities. I know three or four of our big sheep men have been sending their flocks to Fort William for the past two seasons to fatten them on elevator screenings. They figure that it takes about 250 pounds of screenings to carry a sheep through the hundred feeding days. On the basis of the re-cleaned screenings which we could have at Lethbridge, they figure we could increase our sheep by 76,000. In addition to that great benefit for the people of that part of the country, there would be the additional advantage of their being able to feed more poultry, pigs and other stock. It is costing us about $60,000 in freight to send these screenings to Fort William-an entirely unnecessary expense. I do hope the minister will communicate with the Board of Grain Commissioners and see if some method cannot be devised for cleaning a good deal of this grain nearer to the point of production, so that the mixed farmers and sheep growers of the locality may get the advantage of the by-product for their stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I will.

This cracked wheat business is becoming very acute at times; last autumn the condition was the worst that I had ever known. As the minister is himself a miller, will he tell us if it is detrimental to the quality of flour if cracked wheat is mixed with the whole wheat? .

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: My hon. friend can quite understand, I am sure, that the admixture of cracked wheat makes a dark flour which I doubt very much if he would care to buy for his own family needs. Sometimes wheat is cracked in the thresher by incompetent threshers setting the cylinders too close. The miller will not buy cracked wheat simply because he cannot sell the flour produced from cracked wheat.
Would it be practicable to grind the cracked wheat by itself for flour?

There is a world market for flour, if any person thinks there is money [Mr. Robb.3
in dark flour he has every opportunity to try to create a demand for it.
That is the way it works.

That is exactly the way it works; I know by practical experience. In many cases it is the man's own fault because he will not be reasonable and have the fair thing done to him by the thresher. So far as the value of screenings is concerned, I would simply confirm what the minister says. At our own terminal at Port Arthur we burnt as much of it as we possibly could; we had more of it than we could use. As the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans) will remember, down at the head of the lakes they had been dumping the screenings around the trestle work supporting the railway approach to the elevator. Well, the water got in there; the material decomposed, and you could not go within a hundred yards of the elevator without holding your nose; it was worse than any rotten brewery or anything a man could imagine. We had to pay to have that stuff taken away and dumped into the lake. So that the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) will see that when he receives a dollar a ton for his screenings, he is probably receiving more than they are worth.

Item agreed to.
Grant to Canadian Engineering Standards Association for. the promotion of uniformity of standards in metallic and other products, $10,000.

What I have to say on this item might as well apply both to this and the following resolution on the same page with reference to the Honorary Advisory Council of Industrial and Scientific Research. There has been under contemplation for some time the establishment of a Bureau of Standards or a Central Research Institute, and personally I think that is something that we should establish in a very definite manner as early as possible. It would appear from the estimates that we are spending a great deal of money indirectly in this connection, but we might have more efficiency and better results if even a little more money were expended and the bureau or institute established in a definite manner.
With reference to the work of the Research Council, I know of nothing of greater moment to the country at the present time than the fuel question. I listened the other day to a most interesting address by Sir Clifford Sifton and also had an interview with the fuel commissioner of the province of Quebec, Mr. Wanklyn, both of whom have given a great deal of thought' and study to this problem.

The suggestion was made by them:-it is not in any sense original, and I am not advancing it as such-that this body should devote itself during the coming year to research in connection with the fuel problem, and some very practical suggestions were made. For instance, it was pointed out that we were dependent upon anthracite coal from south of the line, and that repeatedly during the last two or three years efforts have been made in Congress and in state legislative bodies to put an embargo upon the exportation of coal to Canada. These are warnings that should not be disregarded. As a matter of fact, the shortage of coal this year has, I -night say, narrowly escaped being a tragedy in some instances. It seems perfectly clear that we cannot, in Canada, hope to depend, for fuel purposes, only on anthracite supplies from the United States. We have an abundance of soft coal, and while it is quite true that soft coal is not as suitable as anthracite for domestic use, it certainly will produce heat and, if properly handled, will serve, perhaps, almost as well as anthracite. On the Pacific coast we use nothing but soft coal; we get along very nicely with it and have no difficulty whatever. On the east coast there is an abundance of soft coal; in Alberta and British Columbia there are unlimited supplies of soft coal; yet in the great central district of Canada, where the industrial concerns are located and where you have congested populations, there is no, coal. The function of government, it seems to me, is to solve a problem of that kind. I do not mean to say that the minister or his department should take that responsibility; but we are spending a large sum of money on this research work, and it seems reasonable to suggest that a problem of that kind should be immediately referred to this body with a definite request that some action should be taken.
I might recite, for a moment, a suggestion made by Sir Clifford Sifton and Mr. Wanklyn. They suggested that there should be established, contiguous to the large centres, such as Montreal, Toronto, Ottawa, Hamilton and so on, coke ovens with the necessary equipment for saving the by-products; that soft coal from the Maritime provinces should be brought to those centres and out of that coal the gas made which, I am assured by some experts, could be supplied very cheaply to those centres for use as fuel; that the coke could also be used for fuel-and coke makes an excellent substitute for hard coal, as it is smokeless and fairly dustless-and in addition to. that, various by-products would be produced which, we all know, are of great

Supply-Trade and Commerce
value. That is a problem which, I suggest with great earnestness to {he minister, might be referred to this body, and if the appropriation proposed is not sufficient, parliament ought to vote a larger sum for that purpose. I look with a great deal of anxiety to the future, if we are to have each year a recurrence of this fuel problem, each year getting more acute and fraught with greater danger to the public, to industry and to the welfare of the community generally. I throw out this suggestion for the consideration of the minister now that we have these two items before us.
Would a discussion on standardization of machinery, particularly farm machinery and the parts thereof, properly come under this head?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.

Then I should like to deal with that matter just for a few minutes. This is a matter of considerable importance, and I should like to see it fully discussed in parliament. In past years, a great deal of difficulty has arisen owing to the fact that even the same kind of implement manufactured by a firm in different years, has parts that are just a little different. For instance, if you break a part of a bindei purchased in 1921, you may find that the part you would buy for 1922 would, perhaps, not just quite fit. If you buy a wagon of a certain make, and a nut or a bolt is lost, you will find that the same part from another wagon will not fit, will not serve as a repair. I have no hesitation in saying that those who manufacture the machinery are not anxious that these parts should fit. We often find ourselves in this position. A part of a binder or a wagon or some other farm implement is missing, or, perhaps, more than one part; we find that those parts are not in the repair shop; we cannot get them, and we are under the obligation of throwing the implement aside altogether, although it may not be nearly worn out, and purchasing a new implement. If something were done to cause the various parts of farm machinery to be standardized, so that nuts and other parts of one implement would readily apply on another as far as practicable - and I think a great deal could be done that is not now being done-much loss and expense would be saved. This is something in which farmers are very much interested. I do not know that I have any positive proof except from conversation with those who should know much more about this matter than I do; but they have told me and given me
sufficient proof that those who are manufacturing those implements are not anxious that the parts should be standardized, and are not likely to standardize them unless they are compelled to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In reply
to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), I might say that in the Mines department, we are taking active steps to test low-grade coals, just by the method as outlined by my hon. friend and as suggested by Sir Clifford Sifton. Early last fall we began to be interested in this question on account of the probability of a fuel shortage in Ontario and Quebec. We have made considerable investigations, and officials of the Mines branch are working on the technical aspects of this problem, in close association with the work of the United States bureau of mines. The problem, as it would appear at the moment, is one of transportation and supply. According to statistics available regarding supplies in eastern Canada -and I speak particularly of the Nova Scotia fields-the probable maximum output of the fields of Nova Scotia would be, if the mines were run at full capacity, about 8,000,000 tons. If a plant were established, say at the city of Montreal, for the conversion of this bituminous coal by the coking process, and the by-products utilized in that city, this would just about supply the necessities of the province of Quebec.	Therefore, the
more pressing problem, that of the fuel supply for Ontario,	will have	to be foundfrom	some	other source,	and wehave	turned	our attention	to those
bituminous fields of the United States that are within three or four hundred miles, say, of the city of Toronto, where a similar plant might be established. Plants might be established also at the other larger centres throughout Ontario.
I should be pleased if it were possible to utilize an all-Canadian supply, but we believe at the moment that that is rather a difficult matter owing to transportation, because the supply would have to be brought from the western coalfields, entailing a haul of over 1,200 or 1,300 miles, if not almost 2,000. The haulage would add so much to the cost that it would render the price practically prohibitive.
The Scientific Research Council has instituted experiments in the briquetting and treating of coal in Manitoba. The Manitoba and Saskatchewan governments, joined by the federal authorities, have for some years been carrying on experiments in the attempt to carbonize and briquette that product. Some-

Supply-Tmdf and Commerce
thing like $800,000 or $900,000 has been expended in this experiment and there is a complete plant established at Bienfait, in Saskatchewan; but so far that experiment has not been successful. Within the last month our attention has been directed to an experiment that has been in progress at the University of Dakota, and we have shipped two carloads of coal from the Bienfait district to that plant. One of our fuel experts witnessed the experiment and reports that they were successful in carbonizing our coal at that particular point. To construct one of these units is not nearly so expensive as the units that have been constructed and which have proved to be a failure at Bienfait. ' About $1,600 will construct one of them. But one of the practical difficulties in the carbonizing process is briquetting, and that problem has not yet been solved. True, in the initial experiments carried on by the Mines branch in a small way on two or three ocassions they were successful in the briquetting process. But so far the development of these experiments has shown that on a large scale these tests are not reliable, and a good deal more remains to be discovered in connection with briquetting.
What my hon. friend suggests has been tried in North Dakota and in the western states, where they have been experimenting with a grate that can be placed in the stoves to burn the carbonized product in its powdered state without briquetting. Of course, they can purchase that product at greatly reduced prices; but after all it is hard to keep for any considerable time. The technical work in connection with these experiments will be carried on. With regard to the problem of coking the bituminous products of Nova Scotia and the area that is contiguous to the central portion of Ontario, that in our opinion at the moment would seem to be the method of solving this somewhat serious problem, so far at any rate as Ontario is concerned.

What success has
been achieved in briquetting peat in Ontario?
I believe that experiments have been conducted for a number of years. Have they been successful to any extent?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Experiments carried on with respect to the utilization of peat as a fuel are not new from the point of view of the methods employed in the older countries of Europe and in the United States. You do hear from time to time that it is possible to dry peat artificially. I am not prepared to deny that. But I may say that Mr. Camsell has visited Germany this year, has
(Mr. C. A. Stewart.]
examined the operation in England, and has consulted with the Bureau of Mines of the United States, and the advice we have received is that it is a somewhat expensive process. Therefore at Alfred, where experiments have been carried on, attention has been directed to the sun-dried process. That involves the perfecting of machinery to obviate* manual labour as far as possible in order to cheapen production. This year, while they have not such machinery as they would like to see installed, they nevertheless have sufficient knowledge, from the experiments that have been conducted over a period of two or three years, to warrant them in the statement that they can successfully manufacture peat and air-dry it at a cost of about $3.50 per ton delivered at the station. One of the difficulties again is the matter of transportation, because the commodity is bulky; and, quoting from memory, I think the rate from Alfred to Ottawa, a distance of some fifty miles, is about $1.40 per ton. It is evident therefore that it cannot be conveyed over very long distances. As a subsidiary fuel of low grade, however, there is no doubt that it would be of immense value to the province of Ontario where there are so many large peat bogs all within fairly close reach of the larger centres. Experience shows that with the machinery now in existence it Is possible to manufacture peat at the price I have quote'd, namely, $3.50 per ton. Of course, it must be remembered that no very large output can be produced, because the season is short, and as the product must be sun-dried, it must be produced and manufactured during the midsummer months. So that if we happen to have wet weather or dark days the output is accordingly reduced.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I want to take the opportunity of impressing on the government the imperious necessity, not of experimenting with this thing or that, but of making certain that we do not in Canada face another winter in the perilous condition we faced this. It is all right to have a lignite board trying various chemical experiments with briquetting and carbonizing lignite. It is proper also to be testing coke ovens, and we may perhaps expect a little there. We may look, too, with a little hope to our peat bogs. These may be all right. In time possibly, in time almost certainly, one or more, maybe all of these will be of real value. But the chances of any one of them meeting a really acute fuel famine next winter are practically nil. This year we came to the verge of winter, in fact we stumbled through it, merely trusting to luck. There was no provision made. We had no definite, reliable understanding with the United States; and we

Supply-Trade and Commerce
found ourselves in the middle of winter with children dying. Unquestionably many lives were lost this winter among the poorer classes, especially in the larger cities, because of insufficient heat and an utter inability to get the means of supplying it. We found ourselves in that condition this winter, compelled to send our representatives to bend their knees to American fuel controllers and beg of them the favour of a little coal. It will not do for this country to be in that position again.
Now you ask, "What can we do?" There are measures we can take so as to be absolutely sure of having coal. We have the coal ourselves. We not only have bituminous coal, we have anthracite as well. We have coal lor all our industrial purposes undoubtedly, but I mean we have coal for the heating of our homes; for this purpose we have a grade of coal just as good as any we import; we have it in Alberta, we have it in British Columbia. The minister says that the freight is high. So it is. But the mining of the coal is very easy. Our anthracite mines are not yet reached by railway facilities, but it does not take very long to construct a railway from the end of steel to-day to one or more of our anthracite deposits; it would not take a heavy capital investment; and I venture this conjecture, that that anthracite can be mined at more than one point at	a cost very little exceeding a
couple of dollars per ton. At present prices of anthracite coal in Ontario that leaves a pretty big margin for the carrying of that coal into this province even to compete against the Pennsylvania product.
But it is not a matter of competition. It is a matter of getting coal, it is a matter of ensuring this country against a fuel famine,
. and against further humiliation. Let me repeat, it is not something to be overcome by merely relying on the precarious success of this or that experiment and talking vaguely of doing something this way or that. It is necessary to take action to ensure, as we must ensure at whatever cost the insurance may be against the people being confronted with another fuel famine next winter. We were not in this danger in years gone by; this last winter has shown us the very real danger we are in.
I have had estimates given me of the actual cost of bringing coal within at least the radius of Nova Scotia coal distribution, and the figures are not such as to make it prohibitive even in competition with the anthracite product. But again, I repeat, whether the figures go beyond the limit that would bring it within the radius of competition with the anthracite product or not, means must be
found to see that we are on a sound basis so far as our fuel is concerned before another winter is upon us.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is
rx anthracite coal within eighty miles of any railway in the province of Alberta.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is eighty miles?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is not
anything. But my hon. friend speaks of the condition last winter. Clearly we could not build a railway eighty miles long during the winter.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Well, my
hon. friend intimated that it was a very small matter, but he perhaps does not understand that it will cost $4,000,000 to construct eighty miles of railway to reach anthracite coal deposits west of High River, which is the nearest Albertan point I know of at the present moment. There is no anthracite coal in Nova Scotia. True, you can bring the product of Nova Scotia into the heart of Ontario during the summer season, but it is a low grade coal and cannot be utilized in our domestic furnaces.
What I was speaking of was not the immediate demand for fuel. It it were a burning necessity, coal could be brought from Alberta to Ontario to-day, but it would be at a prohibitive price. The utmost limit of coal haulage is about five hundred miles. Now, should we not be alive to a problem that is bound to become more serious as the years go by? It is not at all improbable that the Americans will prohibit the exportation of anthracite coal within the very near future. Therefore is it not good business to prepare for that day by the utilization of our domestic product? If we had coal deposits within four or five hundred miles of the city of Toronto, then it would be quite reasonable to devote every energy to bringing it to the central portions of Ontario. But within three hundred and fifty miles we have just the same grade in the United States, bituminous coal of the same character as Nova Scotia's, that can be treated as I have outlined. It seems to me that that is the problem we should tackle at once.
I am not unmindful of the fact, and as a resident of Alberta I would be delighted to think, that we could at a reasonable rate, supply the people of Ontario or any other part of Canada with the immense quantities of fuel that we will have for sale in that province for the next three or four decades. But I think the cost of transportation will make it out of the question. With the product that can be

Supply-Trade and Commerce
secured for the province of Quebec from the coal mines of Nova Scotia, although limited, and with the product that can be secured from the United States without fear of having an embargo placed upon it, treated in the central districts as I have outlined, we will, I think, in a much more reasonable way be able to solve this question from the financial standpoint.
Would the cost of Alberta coal laid down in Ontario be higher than we in the prairie provinces are paying for Pennsylvania coal at the present time-$28 a ton?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh no, I think you could lay down the Alberta product at about $16.50 per ton. That is based on the rates charged from the mines to Winnipeg a year or two ago.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister has furnished the information that exactly completes m.y argument. I want him to understand that I was not objecting to the endeavours being made now in the Mines department and in the Interior department, or to the plans outlined by the minister. How could I? I think I was instrumental in commencing two of them. But the matter has reached such a crucial stage that we cannot rely on such methods. The minister says that we are not in great danger because in a pinch we can bring in Nova Scotia and Alberta coal. But we cannot bring it in in a pinch. That is exactly what I want to drive home to the minister. We cannot bring Alberta coal in here when we get into the depths of next winter at a time when Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta wheat is flowing eastward; we will not have the railway facilities to move coal as well. We can ensure against another fuel famine next winter by getting the coal here ahead of time, and if we can lay it down in Ontario at $16 a ton, that is less than I am paying to-day. If it is possible to burn the bituminous coal of Nova Scotia in our furnaces, well and good, but I do not know. I have heard the present Solicitor General (Mr. McKenzie) display considerable erudition in trying to convince this House that the people of Ontario ought to burn the bituminous coal of his province, and he assured us that they would get far better results at the difference in prices.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: You cannot burn it in grates.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is a difference in the government on that point; but that is not the only point on which there is a difference among them.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Get another grade.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Let the hon. minister take either horn of the dilemma. If we cannot utilize Nova Scotia bituminous coal we have got to build the eighty miles of railway referred to into the anthracite deposits of Alberta. Let the people be warned in time. Let us arrange to get coal from both ends of the Dominion. Do not let us trust to luck, for if we do we are depending on a very slender reed.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have had an experience of sixteen years in connection with the burning of the lignite products of Alberta. I am assuming, of course, that my hon. friend did not say

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not mean lignite- bituminous products, say.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Bituminous is not available. This coal is not more than a semi-anthracite; it hardly falls within the class of the anthracite of Pennsylvania. Tests have been made at the university and elsewhere of all these grades of coal. The difficulty with our product is that you cannot utilize it if it is stored in midsummer-at least, not without great waste, and waste is a very potent factor where such a tremendous freight rate has to be paid. So I want my right hon. friend to realize that it is not all as easy as it looks. He suggests storing the product of Nova Scotia, but you could not burn the product of Nova Scotia in your present anthracite grates; you would have to have special grates. True, it has been done by Mr. Gray, one of the officials of the Dominion Steel Company, but when used in his anthracite furnace it was mixed with coke,, with fairly successful results. There is nothing mysterious in connection with this thing.
I do not think we need experiment on it for two or three years; results can be quickly obtained, but we must start upon definite lines in arriving at a solution. It is not my problem to solve the fuel difficulties of this winter; that was left to another board. My task is to endeavour to solve the problem permanently for this central part of Canada.

I think the minister has mistaken the point of my observations of a moment ago. I do not wish in any sense to cast a reflection on the efforts of the Department of Mines. What I want to point out is that under these two votes we are spending a very considerable sum on scientific iesearch.
I believe the government would get results if they instructed a body of scientists such as we have here to solve this problem, and gave them sufficient money to do it. I am aware of the efforts being made by the Mines depart-

Supply-Trade and Commerce
ment in seeking to utilize these lignite deposits of western Canada. Now, that is a problem-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend is absolutely wrong. The Mines department have nothing to do with that; the Research Council is in charge of it. I hope you will not blame the Mines department for anything in that connection.
My hon. friend will admit that it is under the Interior department that these experiments are proceeding.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, it is not.. Mr. MEIGHEN: It was.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The scientific research body is under the control of the Department of Trade and Commerce. The reports from the Lignite Utilization Board come to the Department of Mines. Within the last year, in order to see that we are getting value for these experiments, we have taken a direct interest in the matter; I have had the deputy minister follow every step of the investigation that has been carried on,

Does that not emphasize the point I am making? My hon. friend gives us quite a lengthy explanation of what is being done to solve the fuel problem; then he says that the experiments are under some other department and that his department is taking an interest in the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Let me put my hon. friend right-

Let us brush away these trivial points. What I am getting at is that we have a fuel problem, and I suggest that the government should definitely instruct the Advisory Council on Scientific and Industrial Research that that problem needs solution and needs it quickly. Half a dozen solutions have been suggested. One is to use a coke oven for the coal of the Maritime provinces; another is to bring in American bituminous coal; another is to bring coal to this part of Canada all the way from Alberta. I will add two more: you can get Welsh coal from Great Britain at a-very low price; I venture to say it can be landed in Montreal just as cheaply as some of the bituminous coal from the United States. Certainly Pacific coast soft coal could be landed in Montreal or at the head of navigation as cheaply as coal from Alberta. So that there are many suggestions to make, but we seem to be rambling around, one department looking at one side of the question and the Research Council looking at another-no one seems to be responsible.
If this vote is not large enough, let us make it large enough to attack seriously and solve this fuel problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
What I
object to is the charge of the hon. member that this is a mix-up affair. I hope I have not misled him to that extent. The experiment at Bienfait was instituted and carried on by the Research Council under the supervision of Mr. Ross, who was chairman of a committee of the council appointed for that purpose. That committee was entirely outside the Mines department or the Department of the Interior or anyone else. The money was voted by Parliament and was expended under the supervision of 9 p.m. that committee until a year ago; in fact, it is still under their supervision.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: To what minister do those in charge of that lignite investigation report, and what minister puts in the estimates? I may tell the minister that when I was there they reported to me; they went over all their accounts with me, and it was through me that the recommendations were made to council.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My right hon. friend is speaking now of the committee?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Of the lignite committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is true I got reports that were submitted to Sir James Lougheed, and ' it is true also that I had to make a, report on this matter last year. But my right hon. friend will not argue that that committee was under the control of the department or took advice from the department?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Oh yes. It is under the departmental control, just as, for example, the old Conservation Commission was under the control of the Department of Agriculture. Its estimates are subject to the recommendation of the minister. It does not take its direction scientifically from the minister, but it is under the control of the government. It is not a commission that is at large and subject to parliament, like the Civil Service Commission. It is responsible to the department over which my hon. friend has control.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Did my
right hon. friend have anything to do with the appointment of this committee?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No. It was appointed before I got there; that is why I did not.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I may be entirely wrong, but that is not the impression

Supply-Trade and Commerce
I got of the matter. That committee was appointed by the Research Council. True, for the purpose of making reports and getting the necessary money, it was placed under one of the departments of government, the Department of Mines. Now, we understand the situation; what I am anxious to point out is that, when I came on the scene no one in. the department that I knew of was willing to take the responsibility for that committee. I do not think that is the best way to spend money, and that is why I have instituted in the Department of Mines this committee of technical men to work on this problem, being under the control of and responsible to the Department of Mines. I have done the best I could to get value for the expenditure made at this plant out west, but in fairness to the Department of Mines I want to' make it very clear that they are not and have not been responsible for these experiments. For the experiments carried on now, however, they will be responsible and the department will be responsible. That is what I have been trying to convey. My hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) says that we are mixed up in this matter. To some extent we are, but I am trying to finish an experiment started by another body.
