I have not, as yet, suggested that the work be taken away from them; I think they ought to be allowed to finish it. But that is not the case in so far as the coking of the coals of Nova Scotia- which I am proposing to-night for the purpose of solving this problem-is concerned. That is directly under the, control of the Department of Mines, and of the minister.

I want to ask the minister a question that is not so greatly involved as the one we are just discussing. I agree with the necessity of beginning now to provide a supply of fuel for the people of this country, especially those in the central parts of Canada, for next winter, and having regard to the necessities of the province of Ontario, and to the fact that there are large deposits of peat in that province, I would ask what the department are doing to make it possible to use these peat deposits in the neighbourhoods where they are located.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know that I can speak of the time when the experiments were started. I may say, however, that the expense is borne partly by the government of Ontario and partly by the federal government, and the experiments were' carried on under the direct supervision of the Mines departments of the two governments. The experiments have been conducted at Alfred, a place about fifty miles from this city, 
between here and Montreal, and I have just announced to the committee that a report has been made to the federal and Ontario governments that they have perfected machinery , that can produce sun-dried peat at $3.50 per ton. I may add that I think that after the technical and scientific part of the experiment has been carried out, it is hardly the business of the government to conduct the commercial end of the undertaking.

I am not very sure that I shall be in order in what I am going to say, but my statement is perhaps very well known to the Minister of the Interior. In regard to Alberta coal I have heard some discussion tonight as to the suitability of grates that have been burning anthracite for the burning of Alberta and softer coals. I do not know that there is any hard coal being burned in the province of Manitoba to-day to any extent outside the city of Winnipeg. A few years ago everyone had to purchase anthracite to burn in his furnace. To-day the people of the province of Manitoba generally speaking, are burning soft coal and experiencing no trouble in the world. I am talking from personal experience. We have had better heating results with coal from the Alberta mines than we ever obtained with anthracite ; that is in the use of coal in the common furnaces.
I have a statement here made by an Alberta miner which may prove of interest. The letter is dated November 24, 1922 and the writer says:
Practically all of the mines in Alberta are closed to-day for want of orders, althongh winter has not commenced yet. There are enough mines in Alberta to practically bury Ontario in coal in six months.
I have no doubt that the present mines, operating full time with their present staff, could ship at least four times the quantity of coal in a year that they are now doing.
The writer figures out-and I have no doubt the minister is familiar with these figures- that coal can be carried from Edmonton to Toronto at $6 per ton. Obtaining coal from this source would provide a tremendous amount of all the year round labour for the Alberta miners. It would also yield a great amount of traffic for the Canadian National railway and, perhaps, would do something towards putting it on a paying basis.
I canot go into the figures to-night, although I have a detailed statment here, as to the rate per ton per mile and the load that a train could carry from Alberta to Toronto.
I am not an expert on the subject but from the figures in my possession I think it is commercially feasible. At any rate it is worth looking into. It seems a strange thing

Supply-Trade and Commerce
that although Alberta has such tremendous resources in coal Ontario to-day should be suffering for the want of that fuel. In the Maritime provinces also there is an abundance of coal. It is just a question of how it can be the most promptly and cheaply transported. The writer of this letter has gone into the matter very accurately, I think, and he makes the statement that the carrying of Alberta coal from Alberta to the western part of Ontario has never been seriously considered by the management of the Canadian National Railways.
I think, perhaps, the greatest trouble with the Alberta coal is the fact of its slacking. Let me say that there are certain of the,mines in Alberta that I know of that keep the coal for months and it remains perfectly whole and perfectly good. In view of the fact that we have the coal and the transportation facilities, is it not worth while looking into the possibilities of carrying that coal over our own National system and perhaps saving to the people of Canada at least $125,000,000 that now goes each year to the United States? By developing our own coal resources, and carrying the fuel to the points where it is reeded, we should provide work for our own people. It is a proposition, in my opinion, that is well rvorth looking into.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There was
a fuel famine about five years ago, and it took a very considerable amount of money and persuasion on the part of the Alberta government to induce the people of Manitoba to bum the lignite coal. It costs to-day about $4.75 a ton for coal on board the car. That is the rate in Alberta at the moment, and it costs about $4.25 a ton to ship to' Winnipeg. That is about the same rate that is being charged for the transportation of wheat. The qost of | transportation from Winnipeg to Ontario would have to be added to the figure as it applies to coal.
Is the hon. gentleman quite sure as to the freight figures to Winnipeg.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. FORIvE: I do not think they are right but if the minister is sure we will let it go at that.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The $4.25?
Unless there has been a reduction in the last year that figure is right.

Coal is hauled in mixed
trains, and in all shapes. If you loaded a train at Edmonton, one of these big heavy trains, it could be hauled very much cheapen in a continuous journey all the way down than
ic could be hauled into Manitoba in the way in which it is now handled. People are very hard on the miners sometimes, but when the men are only working about half time, they require double the wages to maintain themselves and their families and so it becomes very expensive to mine coal under the present conditions. I think very few people are well acquainted with the conditions under which miners work when they complain about the wages the miners enjoy. When it is realized that they lack' employment sometimes for six months in the year the necessity for the prevailing rate of wages is apparent. Now that we have a new management of the Canadian National Railways I think it would be wise for them to look into the conditions and see whether something along the lines indicated could not be done.

Are the Fuel Commission or the government seeking further means to promote the transportation of coal from Alberta to Manitoba? We are very much interested in that. I understood when discussing this matter with a member of the Fuel Commission not long ago th$t coal was brought from as far as 2,100 miles and landed at Winnipeg where it was being used instead of our Alberta coal. I do not know the reason for that, but if there is any good reason, I should like to know it. It is possible that conditions were such as to justify bringing coal from that distance from another country when it could have been purchased only six or seven or eight hundred miles away at the most, from Winnipeg. We have had evidence here tonight that they have been using our Alberta coal and find that it answers the purpose very well. I think there are good grounds for investigating this question. We are in a position in Canada where we cannot afford to ignore any means of keeping money in our own country, employing our own labour, and paying the coal miners and the mine operators for getting this wealth out of the ground. I would like to impress upon the government that it would be worth while adopting measures to facilitate such a development. It is really a serious matter. We in Alberta need the money for our coal just as much as the people in Manitoba need our fuel. If that were done, it would relieve the situation more or less, because the coal that comes in from the United States could then be distributed throughout Ontario instead of being taken up to Winnipeg and the west, which our Alberta coal could supply. I should like to know what the government or the fuel commission are doing along this line, if they are doing anything.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: If this debate will awaken the people of Canada to the importance of the coal situation and prevent them from forgetting as soon as hot weather comes in June that there is another winter ahead, it will be time well spent. I am not prepared to agree with my right hon. friend, the leader of the Opposition, that this has been the first year of coal shortage, or the worst year for getting coal in Canada. Periodically a coal shortage develops in this country.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does the minister say that there has been any year worse than this? Scarcely any one in Canada can get coal.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Nonsense.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I wish the hon. gentleman were in my position. I am not a member of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: But you are not the whole of Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not know why it should be more difficult for me to get it than the ordinary man. Besides, we come in contact with many in just the same situation. This is the first really acute year of a coal shortage in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Not at all.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I would like the minister to visit our cities. There has been no suffering at all till this year but this year there has been widespread and acute suffering.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: There has been suffering, but I contend that this has not been the first nor the worst year, and I am quoting the statements made by coal dealers who should know something about it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is a pretty good year for them.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
We will not quarrel over it. I quite agree that we should try to use our own coal, but there is no use boasting that we have a large coal supply in the West and then freezing through the winter. I am not prepared to go as far as some hon. gentlemen and say that there is anthracite in Alberta, but I am told that there is a very good quality of coal there, and if that were developed it would also be an advantage to our National Railways to move that coal east. So much for coal.
The Lignite Utilization Board is the organization that has control over the experiments at Bienfait in Saskatchewan. The committee of the Industrial Research Council in their report say that they turned over entirely to the Lignite Utilization Board the carrying on 
of research work in that connection. And may I remind my right hon. friend that it was he himself who was responsible for creating the Industrial Research Council, and that it was during his period of administration that this experimental work at Bienfait was turned over by the Research Council to the Lignite Utilization Board? This board is financed jointly by the Dominion government, the government of Manitoba and the government of Saskatchewan.
Like my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), the other evening I listened to the speech of Sir Clifford Sifton, who is a student and goes deeply into these questions, and the thought occurred to me: If this is as good a proposition as Sir Clifford Sifton thinks, it is a great chance for wealthy men to invest their money and go into the business in Montreal. I confess that Sir Clifford Sifton almost convinced me that it would be a paying proposition to float Nova Scotia coal to Montreal, heat that city with the gas derived from that coal, and ship the coke to the country districts, incidentally deriving considerable revenue from dyes and other byproducts. If he was correct, that would be a profitable venture for some business men to go into. I hope hon. gentlemen do not expect the governments of this country, either federal or provincial governments, to put coal into the bins of the people. Surely we have not yet reached that point. The people must do something for themselves, and if miners go out on strike in Pennsylvania and we allow the newspapers to lead us to believe that the strike is going to be settled to-morrow for all summer, and we go on in that expectation, we may find ourselves in the same position next winter as we did this year. I think we should give it out to the people of this country that they must look after themselves a little bit. They cannot always leave it to the government to provide them with coal, and bread and butter. It is a business proposition and the people must look after themselves.
My hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) asked a question about the standardization of parts of agricultural implements. It may interest him to know that two or three years ago the then member for Kent, now a member of the Upper Chamber, brought in a resolution for that purpose and the matter was referred to the Agricultural committee. That committee had the manufacturers of agricultural implements before them and went into the matter very thoroughly, and they did arrive at some conclusion regarding the minor parts of agricultural implements, but they did not accomplish all they desired. My hon. friend says that the government should go

Supply-Trade and Commerce
so far as to force the agricultural implement makers to standardize parts. So far as possible it is very desirable that there should be uniformity of parts, that parts of different machines should fit one into another. But is it in the interest of users of agricultural implements that the government introduce such legislation as the hon. member suggests? You cannot compel the manufacturer of an agricultural implement in any country outside of Canada to make the parts uniform. If you force Canadian manufacturers to do that, you are creating a great monopoly and you are giving the people having that monopoly an advantage in our country by destroying competition which you wish from other countries. Therefore, I am not sure that it would be to the advantage of users of agricultural implements to pass legislation compelling manufacturers to make the parts uniform.

Notwithstanding the fact that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) has asked that the question of coal be laid to rest and the item pass, the .question of the coal supply is, perhaps, one of the most important questions for residents of Ontario at the present time. IjTo one who lives in cities in western Ontario can deny that there has been a very large amount of suffering during the present winter on account of the coal shortage. We have experienced it; we know it. We have not had the coal, and what coal we have had, we have had to pay a very high price for. We hear from people who seem to know and we read in the newspapers that our experience of this present winter may possibly be repeated next year, or if not next winter, then the following winter. This all depends on whether or not another strike occurs in the United States coal fields.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Or in Canada.

Or in Canada. An athra-cite coal strike in the United States is a most serious thing for the ordinary householder in Ontario. It may be that another strike will not occur in those coal fields next summer, or next winter, or for a year or two to come; but there is still a possibility that these strikes will occur. During the last five or ten years there have been a large number of such strikes, and in some of those years we have certainly experienced a coal shortage in Ontario. I believe the seriousness of the coal shortage was greater this year than ever before. In the city in which I live I have had more complaints this year than ever before, as to both scarcity and price, and there is a prospect of this problem getting worse rather
than better. It is one of those questions which we must face in Ontario and in the Dominion of Canada.
I do not take the view of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that it is a question with which the government has little or nothing to do. He should realize that in facing a coal shortage in central Canada, we are facing something in the nature of a national calamity. The people have a right to look to the government for direction, assistance and protection in the matter of a national calamity, and they will look to the government and hold the government responsible. The question which interests us most in Ontario is: What is the government doing as regards this question? What steps is it taking, or what does it propose to do? No one on this side of the House or in any part of Canada would, I think, for a moment question the propriety of the government expending money in experimenting along lines such as those described by the minister to-night. That is well and good but it is highly speculative. It may eventually result in some relief in this country; but it is a very indefinite matter, and the relief may be long postponed. The question is: What are we going to do in the meantime?
If I understood the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) aright as he spoke to-night - he has left- the chamber, I am sorry to say- his proposal is simply that this country could take care of the province of Quebec, which has no coal, if Quebec had the use of the whole output of the mines of Nova Scotia, which output he estimates at about 8,000,000 tons. That, he says, would provide reasonably well for Quebec, and then the problem of a supply for Ontario would arise. I understand, in Ontario, we use some ten or twelve million tons, and we have no coal in our province. The minister says that we cannot bring coal from Alberta to Ontario on account of the long haul. Let me tell him that many cities in Ontario this winter have brought coal from Wales, and the people have been using Welsh coal. It is true we have had to pay a high price for it. If we can use Welsh coal, surely we can use Alberta coal. The Minister of the Interior intimated pretty clearly that, on account of the quality of Alberta coal and the long railway haul, the use of it in Ontario at the present time is hardly a practical question.
What does he propose? He says that there are coal fields in the United States within 300 or 350 miles of Ontario, and an abundant supply of bituminous coal can be derived therefrom. That is the point that rather

Supply-Trade and Commerce
puzzles me. I have read in American papers within the past two weeks that if another strike takes place in the anthracite fields, great distress will be caused in the United States, and the result will be that the whole output of soft coal of the United States will be used in the United States and that Canada will get neither anthracite nor bituminous coal from the United States. That is a condition which must be considered. It may not be a probability; but it is a possibility and one which the government should consider. We are faced with a real difficulty and means must be found to avert it. If the condition arises again next winter as it did this winter; if it becomes more grave next winter, as it may possibly become, the government is bound to take care of such a situation. It is bound to protect and to direct and to assist, and the time to lay its plans is now, not later on in the season, not waiting, as the minister will say, until next autumn, until the acute situation actually arises. Let plans be made now. Give the people a lead in the matter. It is all very well for the Minister of Trade and Commerce to say-
What plans, if any, has the hon. member in mind that should be laid now?

I do not know that I have a definite plan, and I do not know that I would be called upon to explain it if I had one, although I would be glad to do so. But a government in office for the purpose of governing and taking care of the country should immediately get busy and devise a plan. What ran through my mind was something in the nature of coal depots to be established at various points in Ontario. Whether those depots were to be supplied with Alberta coal, or Nova Scotia coal, or Welsh coal, I could not form a very reasonable conclusion. Then, if the difficulty arises, we shall at least be carried through what may or may not be another hard winter. It is the government's work to look after that, and the people of Ontario feel very much interested in this question. Letters have come, I fancy, from Ontario to every member of this House during the present session. I know I have been interviewed. I have had communications, and the question is: Is the government prepared to direct, to undertake, to help, and if so, will it lay its plans now?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I am Sony to detain these estimates, but I imagine we are all speaking at quite a distance from them. I do not rise to discuss this coal question in detail or at 
any length, because at a future time I wish to take it up in connection with the work done by Mr. Magrath and Mr. McCourt during the past year. But I should not like the idea to go out that the United States has not been dealing fairly with Canada in the coal situation this winter or is not dealing fairly now. As a matter of fact northern New York, to put it mildly, has been as hard pressed on account of the lack of fuel as Ontario has been. I know of one instance in which Pennsylvania anthracite was sent from an Ontario town to a town in New York state to help them out. The United States has acted fairly in the matter in every respect, and I have no doubt that hon. members would endorse that statement if they were acquainted with all the facts. It is true that some gentlemen in the United States, I will not call them agitators, did attempt to stop the export of anthracite into Ontario and Quebec. But when it came to a showdown before the authorities they were brushed aside and the export was permitted, Canada receiving, I think, all she had a right to expect under the circumstances.
As to the lack of coal, we all agree that there is a sufficient pupply on the American continent to keep us all warm and provide for all our necessities. But that is not the trouble When the operators and the owners fall out i' makes no difference what supply Providence has deposited in the earth; we do not get it, and that is all there is to it. It does not matter whether the disagreement takes place in Pennsylvania or in Canada, the supply depends on the ability to bring it to the surface and have it transported. And the United States has just as much trouble, notwithstanding its large deposits, as we have in Ontario. Suppose all plans were laid for bringing the coal from Alberta to Ontario; if the same trouble arose in Alberta as in Pennsylvania we should not be able to get coal from that province any more than we could from Pennsylvania, because it would not be mined. I intend to speak at greater length on this subject on a future occasion when I have all the data, but at the moment I want to point out that the root of the trouble does not lie in the fact that there is not a supply of coal close at hand, although it may be in the United States; it lies in the fact that the coal is not produced at the mines. I think we bum about 4,000,000 tons of anthracite in Ontario and Quebec annually, and this year we have had only a percentage of that, so that we have been left in a straitened condition. Some cities, I believe, have suffered considerably, although some parts of the country have suffered to a greater

Supply-Trade and Commerce
extent than others. As a matter of fact the districts I am in touch with suffered less 'this year than two years ago. That, however, is only a matter of comparison. No doubt it does seem queer to people generally that while we in Canada have an immense supply of coal there should be a lack of fuel. My hon. friend spoke about depots. This proposition would be a good one, I think, if the coal to be stored were Pennsylvania anthracite. But some of the coal we have in Canada would not retain its quality when placed in these depots, and that, of course, would make a difference. Some of the coal in Canada does not stand the weather and will not retain its heating and steaming qualities when stored in large piles or exposed to the air for any length of time. And that is one of the difficulties that arise in transporting our coal any very great distance.
A good many of the coal sheds in Manitoba are filled in the summer and the coal keeps all right until winter. 1 do not think it slacks to such an extent as to present any insuperable difficulty.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I did not refer to any
particular coal. I have been discussing the matter with Mr. Magrath a good deal, and expect to have more data. But let me emphasize again that we do not want it to go out from this House that we believe we have been humiliated in the United States or treated unfairly or anything of that kind. Those in the United States in authority over the fuel situation this year treated Canada fairly; indeed, more fairly than many of the people of New York state think she should have been treated. And this fact is due not only to their fairness but to the work done by Mr. Magrath, who has been at the head of the commission assisted by Mr. McCourt and Major Bell.
Now, as to peat. Put not your trust in peat, is my advice. We have large peat bogs in Canada and I have had more or less knowledge of the peat industry for a great many years. While it has been difficult to get moisture out of peat, it has been done, but to such a negligible degree that the quantity produced cannot be depended on to take the place of coal. As an auxiliary, shipped over a few miles, it can be successfully utilized, and it has great heating and steaming qualities. But the quantity produced up to date, under the experiments that have been made, has been comparatively small, and for years to come we shall not be able to depend on it except as an auxiliary. I am in hearty sympathy with the idea that we should work
out some scheme to enable us to use our owe coal, because apart from the possibility of a famine or the difficulty of getting a supply from the United States, Canadians ought to use their own coal so far as they can, simply because it is their own. That is the policy I believe in, and I think that the minister (Mr. Stewart, Argenteuil) has started a useful line of experiments. I have a good deal of faith in the final outcome of these experiments, because if we can utilize Nova Scotia coal or western coal in the form of coke or in any other form in the central sections of Canada, we have not only done something to protect ourselves, but we have accomplished something to the advantage of both East and West and of the whole Dominion. So far as it is possible to do so, my policy, I repeat, is that we in Canada should utilize our own resources.
Is the $120,000 in this item supposed to be for the purpose of carrying on further work in connection with these experiments this summer?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The $120,000, I understand, does not all go to that work. The work is financed by the Mines branch of the Dominion Department of Interior, as well as by the governments of Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
Last year there was a total of $250,000 voted for the experimental work at Bienfait.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That matter comes under another department.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I might answer the question. There was $250,000 voted last year of which $125,000 is still available. Out of that we propose to devote $25,000 to the building of a carbonizer of the same type as that which has just been used in testing two loads of our coal.

There has been a good deal said to-night in regard to the shortage of coal throughout Ontario. The part of the country from which I come is much colder than Ontario and we have had a coal shortage there this year. Since I have had the honour of representing my constituency in this House I have repeatedly requested that transfer switches be placed at pivotal points on the railway for the purpose of having coal transported to our people with regularity. It is a fact, as my worthy leader (Mr. Forke) states, that in western Canada the local coal dealers in the towns fill up their sheds with 60 to 80 tons of coal against the approaching winter, and those whose credit is good can go to the coal merchants and get a sufficient

Supply-Trade and Commerce
supply to fill their bins. But there are thousands of people on the prairies who cannot do that, and these are the people the least able to suffer the hardships of a coal shortage. I maintain that the government in looking after the welfare of the people by protecting them against these fuel shortages should see to it that the railways trasport this coal at lower freight rates. At our lignite mines coal costs from 11.50 to S1.80 a ton, yet when it reaches my home, not more than eighty miles away, I am obliged to pay $7 a ton. I give this by way of illustration. The big spread in price is due to a great extent to the long roundabout haul involving an extra hundred miles or so. It will be readily understood that this is a very heavy toll to take from the people who have to bum this low grade lignite coal.
I do hope that the experimental work will be brought to a success and that eventually we will have the briquetting of lignite coal placed on a commercial basis. About two weeks before I came here one hundred pounds of lignite briquettes were sent me from Bienfait by the Utilization Board. I tried them in my furnace and heater with very satisfactory results. They were a little smoky to start with, but they sgon burned brightly and retained their form until reduced to ash. I see no reason why when another carbonizer is inst'alled and the plant completed a great industry should not be developed that will provide for the fuel needs of the people of the west. I would point out to hon. members from Ontario that they still have wooded areas which can be resorted to in case of fuel shortage, but we on the bleak prairies have no substitute to take the place of our coal-when our coal fails we have to suffer all the hardships of our western winters, and we have been in this deplorable condition many times. I myself have seen a carload of thirty or forty tons of common lignite at a siding, with sixty teams waiting for a supply, being doled out in lots of 500 pounds. The people who go out on the plains to build up the country should receive every encouragement from the government, and their hardships should be reduced to a minimum. And certainly the government should take the necessary steps to ensure these settlers against any further fuel shortage.
Which government?

All governments, whether by co-operation or by individual effort. I am not charging any government with being derelict, but it seems to me the seriousness of the fuel problem in the West has not im-
[Mr. Gould-l	*
pressed itself upon governments to the extent that we consider desirable. We have terminal elevators to store our excess grain until transportation can be provided, and while the hon. minister was speaking it occurred to me that fuel depots throughout the western provinces and Ontario would be a means of solving this problem and would not entail a very heavy expenditure. I would like to see the lignite fields in my district developed. I have been informed that north of the present lignite area there are huge deposits of coal of exceptionally good quality, and I have had many requests from people in that territory for the government to test the extent of these deposits. I think it would be good policy for the Minister of the Interior to give this matter his consideration.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
This is a very familiar question to me and one on which I have been expressing opinions for the last twenty years in and out of this House. For many years I found it difficult to get anyone to appreciate the great importance of the question, because we were not then faced with the prospect of embargoes on our importation of anthracite coal from the United States; we could get it in abundance, and therefore it was difficult to impress on the people of Ontario and Quebec the desirability of our being independent in every respect, particularly in regard to our coal supply.
It is rather disappointing to me to hear the suggestions made that after' helping to develop the hard coal deposits of the United States, and now having reached the stage when we may be denied any further supplies of their anthracite, we should start in to develop their soft coal and continue our dependence for our fuel upon a foreign nation. No doubt they are a very friendly people and quite willing to deal with us while we have the money to pay for the coal they send, us, but the day may come when we will be thrown back on our own fuel resources, and then I am confident we shall regret the extent to which we have neglected to develop our own coal deposits.
Our transportation facilities-our railways and canals-are built with the idea of developing our trade east and west. Now, is it not the sane and proper course for us to utilize these instruments of transportation to meet the necessities of our people, particularly in the matter of fuel supply? I was very much disappointed with the figures given by the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) in regard to the limited production of coal in Nova Scotia. It will be readily understood that
80 i

Supply-Trade and Commerce
every business man has to limit his production or output to his market. That is the situation in the Nova Scotia coal-fields. We have unlimited quantities of coal under ground, but our market is limited; we can sell only 7,000,000 or 8,000,000 tons a year, and consequently the output is limited. But if we can assure the coal owners of Nova Scotia of a bigger market it will be no trouble for them to double their output. Many of the mines now open are only working single shift. With the demand doubled it will be no trouble for those mines to work double shift and produce double their present output, and if this supply is not sufficient to meet the fuel requirements of Ontario and Quebec, more mines can be opened. So hon. members will see that Nova Scotia can produce as much coal as may be	required to	meet thefuel demands	of Ontario	and Quebec or of any other part of Canada. We have in Nova Scotia limitless quanities of coal at tidewater, capable of being transported to any part of this country. But those who have invested money in that business are looking for a proper return from what they have put into it, and it is up to the business men of Ontario and Quebec, and up to the government, so far as they can help in that direction, to arrive at some method by which this coal can be brought into the central provinces and used to meet the needs of the people in the matter of fuel.
A good deal has been said about briquetting. We have passed the experimental stage of briquetting in Nova Scotia. We have briquetted coal; it is a splendid fuel of which hundreds of thousands of tons can be produced in our province if there is a market for it. I imagine it is just as good a fuel as anthracite, particularly in open fire-places; it makes a more cheerful fire, being more like wood fire than anything you can get by using anthracite. We have also passed the experimental stage so far as coking is concerned; we have coked hundreds of thousands of tons of coal, and the product thus obtained has been used in the different cities of Ontario and Quebec with highly satisfactory results. This question is one of the most important that the House has had to discuss, and being an old coal miner myself, I am glad to have this opportunity of saying something with regard to it, particularly with regard to our coal in Nova Scotia. There is talk of having coal shipped to Montreal, and there converted into coke. What is the matter with converting it into coke at the pit mouth? If there is danger from ignition in the yarding of large quantities of coal, that danger does not exist in con-51
nection with coke. In the process of making coke the sulphur is removed and it can be piled mountains high without any difficulty on that score. We should all stand up, more or less selfishly, for the development to the fullest extent of the resources of our own country, and you will pardon me, I am sure, if I express the ambition we have that our coal should be converted into coke in the part of the country in which it is produced, thus giving our people the advantage of that further development. Coke is much lighter than coal; very much larger quantities of it can be carried by water, and the units of heat in your cargo will be much greater than if coal is carried. I suggest, therefore, that the manufactured article rather than the raw coal, be transported and yarded at different centres. Then you will have a fuel suitable for any use, whether for furnaces or for stoves, for heating or for cooking. I am sorry to appear as if I were delaying the estimates of the minister, but this is a very important subject, and I am glad to have an opportunity to express my views upon it. We cannot too soon be independent of outside countries for such a necessity of life as our fuel supply.

I wish to endorse the sentiments expressed in the latter part of the remarks of my hon.
10 p.m. friend (Mr. McKenzie). I wish also to put in a plea for Alberta in this regard, particularly my own district. Out there we have a coal that is, I think, unequalled by coal produced in any other part of the Dominion of Canada. I am told that you can light it simply by applying a match to it, and if you happen to break your looking-glass you can use the glistening surface of the coal as a mirror. It is the most beautiful coal you could see. So far as the shortage in Ontario this year is concerned I must say that I have not seen any very pronounced evidence of it; I did not shiver at all- until I heard the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) speaking. In the West we were not at all alarmed; we did not hear anything about a shortage. However, if a shortage did exist-and it may have; if you have had difficulty in getting coal, it can only be the fault of the people themselves and of this government. We have in Alberta, I say, unlimited quantities of the finest coal in the world, simply awaiting consumers. Are you aware that we are shipping thousands of tons of Drumheller and Taber coal to the United States? If you will only ask us for our coal we shall be glad to send it down to you-if you will pay the freight. The suggestion made by the hon. member for South



Supply-Trade and Commerce
Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) is one that might well occupy the attention of the government. Alberta coal would lend itself to storage in depots; there might be some little slacking, but it would not amount to a great deal. I believe you could get that coal landed in Toronto at around $16 a ton-from $16 to *18, at any rate-and it would compare favourably with the anthracite that is now used in this part of the country. I ask the government, therefore, to consider the possibilities of obtaining for use in central Canada our Alberta coal, particularly coal from Drum-heller. If you will put it up in great storage bins and distribute it as required throughout Ontario, we will supply you with all you need.

I do not know whether the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. McKenzie) was in the chamber when in answer to queries with regard to the advisability of storing Nova Scotia or western coals, the statement was made that these coals would not compare with anthracite so far as quality was concerned; that they would not store without slacking, and that our grates and furnaces were not suited to their use. I would like to hear what my hon. friend has to say in that regard. He knows the kind of furnaces and grates we have here and the kind of climate which exists; he knows whether the coal from Nova Scotia must be used right away or whether it can be stored. I should like very much to get information as to what really can be done with Nova Scotia coal. There is just one other question I want to put to him and that is this: He tells us that Nova Scotia coal can be, and is being, successfully briquetted. I take it that even the Minister of the Interior would not say that Nova Scotia coal in briquetted form could not be used in our grates as they are now. I want to know whether Nova Scotia coal is really being briquetted and what the cost of that coal is.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
As far as the briquetting of Nova Scotia coal is concerned all I can say is that a Nova Scotia company-not the largest of our companies, but a company known as the Bras d'Or Coal Cmpany, and I may say that Senator Currie is the owner of that coal mine-introduced a briquetting machine and made a success of producing the article. But in those days-it was before the war-American coal came in so cheaply that the people did not care to enter upon the experiment of buying these briquettes and the American anthracite coal put the company out of business. In those days you 
could buy anthracite coal and land it in your cellar in North Sydney for $7 a ton. The cost to-day is two and one-half times that price. Even if the briquetted coal cannot be bought to-day the machine is there; they stopped producing briquetted coal because the people would not buy it when anthracite was so cheap and easy of purchase. But there is no ditiiculty in burning these briquettes. I have burned them in the grate in my house and they make a splendid fire. I have been keeping house in North Sydney for the last thirty years and the dwelling is heated by a hot water furnace. I have never burned anything but Nova Scotia coal and the house is clean and comfortably heated. I do not think there is anything peculiar about the furnace it is an ordinary furnace built by people in North Sydney who make a business of it.
With regard to Nova Scotia coal being unfit for dumping as they call it, for many years we had no trouble at all. I believe that a few smaller mines, on the north side of the harbour as well as on the south side, have been opened, where there is a certain amount of shale but there is no difficulty if that is kept out of the coal. If coal with that shale in it is dumped and left for some months there is danger that it will ignite and burn. However, the coal produced by the old standard mines is not subject to this danger at all. In the matter of heating one's house, if there is proper care and proper selection of the coal there is no difficulty whatever.
Let me say to my hon. friend that no matter how good any article is it may be spoiled and given a bad name by being improperly handled. Even a coal miner may spoil coal by allowing shale and stones to enter it, whereas he should keep these materials out. If our Nova Scotia coal is properly mined and handled there is no better bituminous coal on the continent of North America.

My hon. friend did not quite catch the point. I did not want his opinion on the subject of ignition; I wanted to see what his view was as to the statement of the Minister of the Interior that the Nova Scotia coal was of such a character, compared with the lignite of the West that it would not stand; not that it would not burn but that it would slack and become dust and greatly deteriorate in value if exposed to the weather.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Any bituminous coal will suffer more or less when exposed to rain and

Supply-Trade and Commerce
sun. Much will depend upon how long the coal is left out under the weather. If covered up in some sort of a shed this slacking process will not happen at all. If that process takes place it is due to the influence of rain, frost, hot sun and so forth which disintegrates the coal. But even if Nova Scotia coal slacks it is a good fuel. It is not as nice to handle, but you can get a fierce fire, a good heat, out of slack; it never gets to the stage where it is not heat producing.
Washed coal, for the purpose of making steel is treated in washing plants. That means that the coal is ground into what may be called very poor slack, and then it goes through a washing process. Of course you would not use washed coal for heating your house but it gives the best kind of heat in the making of steel. I have been living in the neighbourhood of coal mines all my life and I never saw any Nova Scotia coal that could not be used for heating purposes if used under anything like favourable conditions.

I do not want to add very much to the length of this debate, but while this particular item may be passed without exhaustive consideration the discussion which has grown out of it has really an importance that just at first, I am sorry to say, perhaps some members of the administration did not care to attach to it. We do not want to launch into schemes that are too paternal but on the other hand I do not want to see the government avoiding such measures as may be necessary in order to grapple with really unfortunate conditions which may confront our country. I think that is what a government is for. I think that in a matter of this kind, instead of expending ourselves in mere criticism, if we are given the opportunity it should be the work of each member of the House to make such suggestions as he can for the improvement of the very lamentable situation which we have had to face during the present winter, and which has had to be faced during some previous years.
I am not going to debate whether this is the worst of all the occasions. Personally I think it has been. I may be wrong about that, but I know that the winter has been more severe than any winter in which we had a fuel shortage previously. But we will not get very far by debating that at length. The real question is, what has been done up to date, and what can be done for the future? I do not think that a House that complacently sits for six or seven hours during the discussion of daylight saving, as we did last year, or of a man's spiritual or moral welfare, as
51i
we have done more recently, ought to deny at least a few hours of consideration for a man's bodily comfort. I am not half so anxious to prepare a man for the next world as I am to keep him tolerably comfortable while he is in this world, and some people not in parliament will do all that is necessary to look after his spiritual welfare. Let us here devise the means for looking after his material welfare. To keep him decently warm is one of the most important things.
How is this coal or fuel of whatever nature it may be, to be got? I will tell you what I have seen in my own province, and I presume the same thing has 'been going on all over Canada. It is not bad so far as it goes, not at all bad, but it has simply been the giving of warnings to the people through the press that they must not expect to get American anthracite. In my province we have been leaning very heavily on American anthracite. It has been tolerably cheap; it is a more comfortable fuel than the native product of Nova' Scotia and to some extent of New Brunswick, and our people have used it very largely. They have got warnings that they cannot count on a continuance of the supply. There is not involved in that the slightest bit of reflection on our neighbours to the south. They are doing the best they can in the face of a very difficult situation, and I agree with hon. members of this House who have acknowledged that the United States has dealt fairly with us. But they may continue to deal fairly and still be unable to deal with us even as well as they dealt this winter. When that day comes, will it be enough to use the printing presses to warn the people of this country, to send out circulars to tell them that in all probability American anthracite cannot be got, and that Welsh coal, Scotch coal, stovoids and several other substitutes may be used which will do pretty nearly as well as anthracite, or literature such as I have seen saying that you can make soft coal do very well by burning buckwheat with it? That does not mean the buckwheat that the farmer grows, but a particular size of coal they use down there.
It is easy to say that you can use these things, but what are you going to do to get them? Can you rely on the coal trade? They cannot manage everything. Their importations of anthracite are shut off, and a man who has been dealing in anthracite all his life is perhaps scarcely in a position to make arrangements with mines. He can buy his product so far as it goes, but would it not be better to have a governmental agency spending perhaps a little less time and a

Supply-Trade and Commerce
little less money on finding out how to make analine dyes just for the present, useful as they may be, and put that energy into coordinating the fuel business of the country, just as you would co-ordinate any other enterprise of the country during war time. For this is a war against one of the worst elements with which man has to contend, a war with cold, and he must have his weapons ready.
Is it asking too much of a government that it should function in a matter of this kind, that it should provide leadership, that instead of merely giving out pamphlets, it should have an organization which would be in touch with the men in the coal business, and that means be taken at least to take a rough census of the necessities of the country? For instance, you go into a city like Ottawa. A very brief census will reveal what I will call the institutions whose heating arrangements are capable of being easily made over so as to use fuel oil, other heating arrangements, that can take some of these made-up forms like briquettes, and others which must have anthracite. Then you ration. But it is not enough to ration until you know you have the substance to deal out. Then co-ordinate with the mines and with the railways and see that the necessary material for that particular community is brought in. Leave it in private hands just so far as you possibly can. Do not interfere with the ordinary business of the country more than you can possibly help; but help the ordinary business of the country, help it to stay on its feet and do the work it has to do. Put the force of the government back of it to the extent at least of obtaining information and give them enough power to see that the coal dealer acts justly. It might be necessary to go further, and it being the case of an emergency I would not revolt against even some paternalism on the part of the government. I would even rather have a little grandmotherism than have no action taken at all. What we want to have is the happy mean. I would therefore suggest that some attention might be paid, and perhaps it is being paid now, to the development of oil shales in New Brunswick. I believe a good supply of oil could be obtained there. It would be worth while to help in some way that industry to be developed rapidly, so that oil fuel would be available wherever oil fuel can be used, and it can be used in a great many cases. It is quite a simple matter, I understand, to adapt furnaces of a certain character to the use of oil. But somebody must do those things.

This is as vital to us as any subject I can possibly think of. It is of immensely more importance than nine-tenths of the subjects we discuss in this House, yet to-night it was rather intimated to us that it would be better to let this stand over till some other time, and that anyway, there was nothing the government could do about it. I do not agree with that. I am not taking this position at all from any standpoint of partisanship. I believe the government can do a very great deal about it. I do not believe it is the office of government as one government said of itself, that it was merely a fly upon the wheel and could not control the motion. It did not control the motion, it was a fly upon the wheel, and as soon as the people got an opportunity they replaced it with a government that did something. I am not issuing an invitation to my hon. friends to take measures to remain in power, but I am quite willing, even if it helps them to stay in power, to give assistance by voice or vote in this House in order that they may get courage enough to grapple with this situation and keep helpless people from being frozen to death, for that is what the thing comes down to.
Now I want to say a word about the remarks of the Solicitor General (Mr. McKenzie). New Brunswick coal is good. That coal stands out. I have seen it standing out all winter at the Canadian Pacific coal dumps in West St. John, and it does not slack too much to be used in the engines. There is no danger there. It can be burnt in practically any furnace. Some slight changes are sometimes necessary, and even if sometimes your grates are burnt out by the use of it, what is the cost of a few grate bars compared with the ruin of the health of a family and the ruin of the building itself through want of heat during our rigorous winters?
That is what we come down to; that is the thing to be faced. I am just going to ask the department to enter upon this thing with a whole heart and a willing mind, and to put into being an organisation that will go a good deal further than the organisation has gone this winter; that will reach higher up, that will bring producers and distributors together, that will make a census of the requirements of Canada, and that will make our supplies go just as far as they possibly can. The department may go even further than that. If there is to be a long railway haul in some instances, let them put the new board of railway experts to work. This will be just one more problem for them. I would suggest that they might even lay off for a time the special trains that will be necessary down in my province to

Supply-Trade and Commerce

conduct the second deportation of Acadians from the Maritime provinces, and they might use those trains to better advantage in hauling coal to warm the Canadians of the upper provinces.

I think if we are going to run true to form to-night, we shall have to switch back to standardisation. We carried on the discussion for a while on standardisation; then we went over to coal; then we went back to standardisation, and then over to coal again. I am inclined to think, if we were able to bum within the next ten years all the coal we have been handling since eight o'clock, we would have very warm winters in Canada.
I should like to make a few remarks in reply to the minister before this item passes. The minister referred to a meeting which had been held, to which I understood him to say the agriculturists had been invited, to discuss this question of standardisation. I do not know that my information is correct; but I got the impression from some conversations I had at different times that the way those meetings worked out was this. Manufacturers of farm machinery, not wishing to do certain things, would say that they could not be done, and the agriculturists present, not being practical machinists or engineers, could get no further. Perhaps a different policy on the part of the government, if they wish to progress along this line, would be to have practical men deal with practical men; that is men who are machinists, who know all about the business of making machines, to deal with those who are now engaged in the business of manufacturing machines. The minister took objection to coercive legislation. He doubted whether it would be wise to force those machine companies to take that course. In case an investigation were to prove that the machine companies of Canada, as has been alleged by many, are, for the purpose of making greater gains, multiplying parts unnecessarily, and refusing to standardise those parts when they could very readily be standardised; if that be the case in order that they may sell more machines and reap greater profits, I should like to ask the minister what the remedy is, if it is not coercive measures on the part of the government. It is quite obvious that purchasers of machines could not possibly bring about any remedy by co-operative means or any other, so far as I can see. This would be no departure from what is being done. We have plenty of precedents for coercive measures. I remember some legislation that was passed a short time ago in Saskatchewan in regard to selling machines, and now we
find that a company that sells an engine and guarantees that that engine will develop a certain power, is compelled to live up to its guarantee. Moreover, when they sell machinery, they must use a certain form of contract specified by the legislature. They are also compelled to charge the same rate of interest after maturity as well as before. So in many ways, we have measures that are coercive. Therefore, if it is proved that machine companies are causing a great deal of loss and inconvenience to those who till the soil, and that this is reflected in other lines of business, causing a loss to Canada as a whole, coercive measures will be quite justified.
Since the hour is late, let me close with just one more remark that I was going to make in regard to another matter, perhaps, not quite relevant to the discussion, but a matter of great importance. I refer to the enormous cost of parts. I have heard it said by those who have done some figuring, that a binder that can be bought for about $329 or $330, which, I think, was the price a year or two ago, would, if purchased in parts, cost about $1,500. While I would not say that those figures are exactly correct, I believe they are not far from correct. Those are matters in which tillers of the soil are perfectly helpless. It seems to us that we are in the stranglehold of those who sell us the machinery and provide the parts. It was necessary for the government of Saskatchewan to pass legislation compelling those machine companies to keep the parts, because they practised in the past selling a machine and then within a year or two saying: "We have no parts for that machine; we are not making it any more," and a man with a practically new machine, a machine very little used, was compelled to throw it aside. In order to protect the buyer the government of Saskatchewan was compelled to pass such legislation. This would be going just a little further, and I think it would be quite justifiable. If I thought there was any danger of our switching back to coal, I would talk until eleven o'clock; but as the hour is late, I think we are about ready to pass this item and I will say no more.

I have a good deal of sympathy with the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle (Mr. Millar). I have been interested for many years in this matter of standardization of parts, and I think it is really time that something should be done. Perhaps the hon. member is not aware that last year the Committee on Agriculture appointed a special committee to go into that matter. They picked up the threads that had been dropped

Supply-Trade and Commerce
at some previous session when a special committee had been appointed for that purpose, and they got to the point where they came to a "gentlemen's agreement" with some of the manufacturers. As far as I understand the matter, this was not very much, but just a start that was made. I think three of the companies in Canada agreed to take a certain standard for some bolts and, I believe, knife heads of mowers and certain things like that, and at any time changes were made in the future, they would hold to that standard. That is, perhaps, all right in a way; but the question arises as to other makes coming into the country. The minister mentioned that matter himself. I would suggest that if it were necessary to take any coercive measures, I would take measures which applied not to the manufacture but to the sale. In this way, the measures would apply to implements coming in from the United States as well. The John Deere Plow Company makes a special class of machine for western Canada, a particular kind of plough that, I believe, is not sold in other parts of the country at all. Yet to suit conditions in western Canada, they make a particular class of machine, and any other company will do the same thing. I think the matter is being seriously considered in several states to the south; in fact, I believe in at least four states, there is a law at the present time as regards standardization of sleighs and cutters. The companies are compelled to manufacture and sell only the standard wagon size, I understand, for the convenience of automobiles travelling in the winter time.
One of the secrets of Henry Ford's success is the system of standardization he employs. You will go into one of the Massey-Harris agencies in a small town for some mower sections. They have none in stock and you step across the street to a Deering or a McCormick or a Frost and Wood. You find that they all have these parts, but there is a difference of 1/16- or l/32nd of an inch, just enough to prevent them from working. It seems absurd that such a condition should exist. One particular company makes a practice of changing some of its parts every three or four years and I have been told that this is done with the intention of frustrating the specialty companies who make a business of manufacturing these parts. The only way to get ahead of the specialty companies is to adopt the Ford method, that is, of underselling them. This is a matter that might be referred to the agricultural committee for consideration.
Now, I want to deal for a moment with the coal situation which is after all the im-
[ Mr. Campbell.]
portant question. In the district from which I come we are not particularly concerned with the shortage of fuel. If it is a cold day and there is a lack of fuel all you have to do is to take an axe and go into the bush and bring back some wood with you. There is no trouble in that regard. But I realize the importance of this subject from the national standpoint, and it seems to me that the solution of the whole problem is a matter of transportation. They have an abundance of coal in Nova Scotia, according to the Solicitor General (Mr. McKenzie) as well as in Alberta, and I see no reason whatsoever why it cannot be profitably transported to Ontario and Quebec. I think a good deal of the difficulty could be overcome by making seasonal rates on the railroads. Any practical railway man knows, in fact, one need not be a practical railway man to know, that an engine can haul about twice as much in the summer as in the winter. The time spent-on the road and about terminals is a great deal less in summer than in winter and it can safely be said that you can operate the railways on 35 cents in the dollar during the summer as compared with the winter. One of the problems on the prairies is that as soon as the wheat starts to move the coal begins moving also, and unfortunately in the same direction. When the channels are all clogged with wheat that is the time people find they need coal; and there is no reason why coal cannot be transported in the summer. Mr. Hanna giving evidence before the special rates committee last summer, stated that if the railways had steady business all the year round they could operate with 5,000 box cars less. Now, 5,000 box cars, according to my calculations are worth $25,000,000, and I assume that with engines and other equipment it is necessary for the Canadian National Railways to maintain about $50,000,000 extra equipment. Taking the overhead charges, depreciation in value, interest, etc., I believe I am not far wrong when I say that it will run to $10,000,000 more loss yearly. If that or part of it could be saved by keeping the railways busy all the year round you would accomplish one of the biggest things in the country; you would solve one of the greatest problems that face us to-day. It would also help to a large extent to solve the wage question.
Some hon. gentlemen mentioned conditions with regard to miners. I am more familiar with railway matters than with mining, but I may say that the wage question is also one of the serious problems in connection with the railways. We see a good deal in the news-

Supply-Trade and Commerce
papers about the enormous wages drawn by train and engine men and others employed by the railways. As a matter of fact, however, some of these men very often do not get enough to break even on. They will make a good wage in the fall and winter and most of the summer they are laid off. I know that last summer some men who had been fourteen years in the service of Canadian National Railwaj^s were laid off. That is a serious situation and these men must necessarily ask for high wages if they are to make a living. If you can keep the wheels of transportation moving in the summer-and that I contend can be done by fixing a sliding scale of rates, to go into effect on the 1st of May and be operative until the 1st of August when the grain starts to move-it will give the people in this part of the country an opportunity to secure coal either from Nova Scotia or Alberta, and in many cases some grain cpuld also be carried at lower rates. This would simplify the whole proposition, and I contend that the suggestion ought to be taken into consideration. The transportation of, say, 7,000,000 tons of coal from Alberta would call for about 5,000 trains, and I think the railways are capable of handling it. I would assume from the figures quoted by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) that Nova Scotia can supply 8,000,000 tons, which would leave 7,000,000 tons to come from Alberta. In the year 1922, we purchased from the United States 15,000,000 tons of coal, for which we paid, I think, between $75,000,000 and $100,000,000 or $125,000,000. It seems to me that there is no reason whatever why we cannot save that money and increase the earnings of the Canadian National Railways.
I think that we have overlooked another important source of supply, however. We have looked to the East and to the West,'but we have not looked to the North. I think most hon. gentlemen here are aware of the fact that in the islands along the northern part of Hudson bay there are immense coal deposits, and I am one of those who predict that as soon as the railway reaches James bay it will be found that that coal can be easily brought into Ontario. Looking over a report the other day of Captain Bernier I saw the statement that he had mined coal on Melville island and found it as good as Sydney coal. And there was an abundance of it too. Mr. Stefansson mentions the same thing. I see no reason therefore why we should be dependent on the United States or any other country for coal. They evidently do not want to give it to us, and so far as I can see we could be independent of them if we adpoted the proposal I make of establishing seasonal rates.

Some hours ago in the debate, the Minister of the Interior (Mr Stewart) made the remark that having regard to the ever-threatening danger of the United States putting an embargo on coal coming into Canada, it behooved the government, or it was the intention of the government, to seek to develop and enlarge the fuel resources of Canada. He might also have added, to preserve the existing coal resources. I heartily agree with him in that position, and I have been pleased to-night to hear hon. members from Ontario describe the hardships to which they have been subjected through lack of coal in the East, because perhaps they will now pay some attention to the coal situation in British Columbia, which I brought to their attention last year. My plea at that time fell on deaf ears; but when it is a case of "coming home to the hangman" perhaps they will take more interest in the subject.
I want to mention briefly what the situation is, which is more acute than it was last year, in connection with the mines in Vancouver island and in British Columbia generally. In spite of all this coal scarcity in Canada they are going out of business from want of orders -not from any want of market-due to the encroachment of fuel oil imported from the United States with a very small duty. But for fuel oil there would be enough demand to keep the mines working 75 per cent more than they are working at the present time. But the mines in some cases are working only two days a week, while in other cases they are shut down, on account of the competition of imported fuel oil. The miners in these mines, with all the dangers which they have to face-50 having been killed the other day -are paid a very modest wage. So that the trouble is not due to excessive labour cost. The mines are run in a thoroughly modem and efficient manner. In one case there is not a steam boiler in the whole mine; it is all. run by electricity generated by waterpower. But the trouble is that the coal mines cannot compete with the cheap fuel oil 'which is sloughed off on the market from the American producers of gasoline.
Now, what happens to any industry when it gets down to habitually working only two or three days a week? As you can imagine, large capital is tied up, and it means that those interested will quit. That is what ultimately must happen; they will go out of business.
And what happened a few years ago? These are deep mines, and if not worked they soon

Supply-Trade and Commerce
flood. A deep mine when flooded is about as costly to re-open as to develop a new mine. So when these deep, costly, highly equipped mines go out of business they go out of business for all time, once they become flooded. What happened two years ago may happen two years hence. Two years ago, owing to some economic disturbance in the States-no threat of war or anything of the kind-the sellers of fuel oil notified British Columbia consumers that in three months time there would be no more oil exported into British Columbia. What did the railroad and manufacturing people do? They hurriedly converted back their plants to coal burners, and very glad they were to find the coal mines of Vancouver Island waiting patiently and ready and eager to fill their wants. But in a very short time industrial conditions in the States changed and fuel oil was once more available. Immediately the consumers, selfish, as most business interests are, converted back their plants to the somewhat cheaper and more convenient method of using oil.
Let me predict what will happen two years hence after the coal mines have been shut down. Owing again to some economic disturbance, or to a threat of war or to any other reason whatever-no reason was given last time, none may be given in the future-. supposing the United States again put an embargo on fuel oil? A few years ago we would have laughed at an embargo on anthracite coal, would we not? But to-day it is in sight. They may put an embargo on fuel oil, but by then our mines, owing to our selfish neglect, will have gone out of business. Where will our railways, our ships, and manufacturing industries get their supply of fuel then? There will not be any. What will be the position? Suppose war threatens with some nation bordering on the Pacific, what will we do when our oil supply is cut off and we have no coal to resort to?
Last year I pleaded with the House to put a duty of two cents a gallon on fuel oil in order at that time to preserve our coal industry. I thought it worth while not to let one of our Canadian industries go out of business. This year I no longer plead, I threaten and warn this House and the government that in two years or less our railroads, our ships and industries may be desiring coal and will not be able to get it. It will not then be the loss of the industry, it will be the fact that we will be throttled as a nation, for we will not have any fuel supply in British Columbia, and that is of far greater national importance than even the destruc-
Mr. Neill-1
tion of this single industry. Therefore, I suggest and urge upon the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) that he consider once again the national importance of imposing such a duty on fuel oil as will enable these coal mines to' be kept in operation at least to meet our future wants. Otherwise when the day of travail comes upon us and finds us with no fuel, we as a nation will bitterly regret the selfish indifference we have displayed towards the situation out there.
Mr. Chairman-

Does the committee realize that considerable latitude of discussion has been allowed by the Deputy Chairman? I do not want to shut off the hon. member, but I would remind him that the item now under discussion is No. 367.
My intention was to revert for a few moments to the standardization of fuel oil. I believe I am in order.
Yes.

A matter of great importance to the whole Dominion is the standardization of gasoline and fuel oil. It affects not only those who drive motor cars, but those who operate machinery. In making an analysis of a large number of samples of gasoline and kerosene we find that the specific gravity, distillation and other specifications vary to quite a large extent. We find in many cases that when the weather gets cold retailers fill their tanks with a low grade gasoline and sell it at the same price as they charge for the high grade. I think that consumers should be protected from this fraud by making the oil companies declare the specifications of their commodities. I am told that it is very difficult to standardize these products so as to ensure the importation of, say, gasoline of a certain grade on account of conditions obtaining at the oil wells and distilleries; but it seems to me it would be a very simple matter to compel the companies to guarantee their products to be up to a certain standard; that is, if I buy gasoline I should be able to see at the plant or filling station the actual specifications and so know exactly what quality I am being supplied with. I make that suggestion to the government in order to guard our consumers against the gross fraud now being practised on them.
There is room, too, for research work in connection with lubricating oils. I am convinced that more engines are destroyed from the use of poor lubricating oil than from any other cause. While we have specifications for lubricating oil as to its flash test, viscosity,

Supply-Trade and Commerce
and so on, yet there is something in a lubricating oil, a greasy quality, that we have not yet been able to define exactly. Therefore I think the research branch might well direct their attention to the subject. If they could frame a standard specification for lubricating oils a great deal of fraud would be prevented, for we would then know what we were buying. In addition to the regular oil companies handling heavy oils jobbers are springing up here and there and putting on the market oils of very inferior lubricating qualities. We also find that the dealers in many cases carry three different grades of lubricating oil, and if they get out of one grade before your can is filled they will take the rest from some of the cheaper grades, but charge you the higher price just the same. I should like the government to take this matter into consideration and see whether there is not some way of protecting the consumer from these frauds -for I claim they are nothing less than frauds.
I would like to see the government find out something more about lubricating oils-what the quality of the oil is that makes it a lubricant, and so on-so that the consumers may be protected from every point of view.
