This matter has already been
under review by the officers of the department, but I will again direct the observations of my hon. friend to the attention of the Research Council with a view to seeing whether we can arrive at a basis for establishing a standard for Canada.

The discussion seems to
have gone very far afield; in fact, I have had some difficulty in finding out what item we are considering. There was one matter in connection with the discussion on fuel that impressed me as requiring a little more notice. The hon. minister stated that the steel was within 80 miles of the anthracite coal mines in Alberta. If that coal is really anthracite and compares favourably with Pennsylvania coal, it strikes me that 80 miles is a very short distance to bridge in order that the supply may be made available for Ontario. The hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Copp). according to Hansard of February 21, reports that about 2,700,000 tons of anthracite eoa1 were imported into Canada last year; and that was only about 60 per cent of our normal supply. That would, figuring it roughly, amount to a weight of about 100,000,000 bushels of wheat at 60 pounds to the bushel. If all our western railroads had for every 80 miles of track a business of 100,000,000 bushels of wheat, they would be in a much better financial condition than they are today. The government, therefore, might very
well take into consideration the matter of linking up the rail connections so as to provide us with adequate supplies of our own Canadian coal. The question of freight rates might be submitted to the Railway Commission with a view to securing special rates at certain favourable times of the year so that solid through trains of coal might be taken from the coal fields to, say Fort William, at a much reduced CGst for transportation.
Coming back to the item under discussion.
I have had the honour to be appointed a mi mber of the subcommittee of the Committee on Agriculture, dealing with the standardization of parts. There was very little done last year; in fact we met once and had a little discussion, and that was the end of it. The work already done has been a start, but a very small one. Certain agricultural implement makers have Agreed to adopt certain standards of bolts, and so on, but they are the standard bolts already made, so that there is very little advance in that respect. The question of standardization involves many considerations. The matter of patenf rights is involved; the matter of standardization of machines and parts which come from the United States is involved. In order to make some progress in the matter I wrote to the United States Secretary of Commerce, Mr. Hoover, in August last, and was informed bv him that the American manufacturers of farm implements had taken up this matter of standardization. I will quote a section of his letter:
National standardization as a part of the programme of this department is still in the initial stage of its development however, the farm implement manufacturers having recently appointed a committee to carry forward in surveying present conditions and in recommending simplifications.
I fully agree with you that standardizations of Canada and the United States should be in agreement, particularly in such important fields as farming equipment, and I am asking our Division of Simplified Practice to keep you fully informed as this work progresses. Meanwhile, the most accurate statement of present standards can be obtained from Mr. H. J. Sameit, Secretary of the National Association of Farm Equipment Manufacturers, and we are asking him to give you a statement of these practices.
I have several letters on this subject; I quote from one dated December 23rd last:
Our plow and tillage implement department has formulated its recommendations, and when approved by 75 per cent of the membership who manufacture this line, such recommendations will be ready for adoption, after being formally approved by our General Standardization Committee and the General Executive Committee.
We will be pleased to provide you with the recommendations of each department as soon as they have been formally approved by the General Standardization
Committee and our General Executive Committee. If you desire to have the information piecemeal, wre will forward it.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
I understand that this movement in Canada was started by the farmers, but in the United States it was started by the implement men, the object being to reduce the number of implements that were manufactured for certain purposes, in order that fewer lines of machinery would have to be carried, with resulting decrease in the cost of production. I am not just sure that standardization can be carried very far. It can be effected in many respects, but it can be carried so far that it will lead practically to the stifling of inventive genius. It strikes me, therefore, that a government standard machine is a thing which is a long way in the future.

I understand there is a charge made for the inspection of public scales. Does this charge meet the cost of the work?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: For many years this department showed a loss; this year, for the first time since its organization, there will be a small surplus.

I wish to get some information from the minister bearing upon the answer to a question put in the House regarding the Peterborough district. It would appear that this district is practically self-supporting-in fact, more so-but it is possible that the figures do not cover the whole cost. When the question was put as to what percentage of the moneys collected by the inspector was received by the government the answer was given 100 per cent. The sum of $892 was collected and I would ask what was paid out in cartage.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Is that in Peterborough or in the Belleville district?
The question placed on the order paper had reference to the inspector of weights and measures for the Peterborough district, but I believe this is the same district as the Belleville district.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
It is the Belleville district.
I have not at the moment the details my hon. friend wants but I will be glad to get that information for him.

When a gasoline pump is tested by the inspector and the pump is shown to be short, or does not give a gallon, is there a prosecution for short measure? In the gathering of something over thirty samples of gasoline in the province of Manitoba-a gallon being collected at each station-I think there were only two stations in the entire list where there was a clear gallon; the remainder were all short.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The government's responsibility is inspecting the accuracy of the machine; we are not responsible for the operation of the machine. If there is a shortage I submit the question of prosecution is a provincial one.

Is there a standard cartage charge? As I understand, the inspector goes into a town or village and inspects the scales in rotation, and that it is the practice to charge $2.50 for cartage in each case. The complaint has been made that sometimes this charge is excessive; that there is no reason to make a charge of $2.50 for cartage when the inspector simply goes from one door to the next.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The cartage charge would vary somewhat in proportion to the size of the weights that the inspector had to carry about. It might also vary in different localities. My hon. friend will understand that there might be places where the charge for cartage would be less than in other communities. Of course this matter is governed by regulations and my hon. friend will understand that we do not carry those regulations around in the record. However I will get my hon. friend the information he desires.

With regard to the point raised by the hon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Milne) I have had very grave doubt in my own mind for some time as to the advisability of the department allowing the use of these pumps to measure gasoline or oil. For instance, the inspector may inspect them and they may be perfectly all right, but there is a possibility that the valve of that pump may

Supply-Trade and Commerce
vary the least bit. Gasoline is something that escapes very readily if the valves of the pump are not just as they should be. Then there is a want of suction and you will not get the amount of gasoline you should get. I found on one occasion that the man had put twelve gallons into the ten gallon tank of my car. I told him that I did not mind paying for the gasoline, but I did not want a ten gallon tank stretched by putting twelve gallons into it. How often this thing happens we do not know, and it is worthy of the minister's consideration as to whether the use of these pumps should be continued. They are very convenient, I admit, and one of the things put forward in their favour by salesmen themselves is the fact that they will save their price on the machine in a very short time.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: My hon. friend knows-he is more familiar with the facts than I am-that there are many varieties of this pump on the market. In some cases the department has refused to recognize them. I am not sure, however, whether we should accept the advice of my hon. friend and not inspect them. Perhaps they require inspection oftener. I can quite see that there is a chance for some fraud to be practised.
How often are they supposed to be inspected?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Once a year, but if there is a complaint they are inspected oftener.
If fault is found, is the license refused until the matter is put right?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: They are not allowed to weigh on a scale unless it has been put right.
Would the same rule apply to a pump for oil after it is inspected?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I think so.

I do not think that once a year is often enough to make an inspection. There is another thing. How many drivers of automobiles, for instance, are in a position to know just how much gasoline has been put into their tank? You seldom have your tank empty. Very few people are in a position to gauge accurately what was in their tank when they began to fill it and what it contained when they were done. I know on the occasion I spoke of I said to the fellow: "There must be something wrong with your pump." He took a gallon measure and pumped it out and it was about two-thirds full. Apparently he was astonished himself and said "I will not use that any more."

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I will bring this matter to the attention of the department and see if we .cannot adopt a more satisfactory method.
Is any certificate issued to the owner and operator of a pump after it is inspected?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The inspector places a stamp on the machine and it is sealed.

the House I desire to move:
That it be resolved that a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint their Honours that this House doth agree to their Address to His Excellency the Governor General, respectfully requesting that His Excellency will be pleased to transmit our joint resolution to the President of the Republic of France approving the government's acceptance of the gift made by the government of France of a tract of land on Vimy Ridge for the erection of a monument commemorating the exploits of Canadian soldiers in the Great War, in such a way as to His Excellency may seem fit; by filling in the blank space therein with the words "and Commons".
